item.title: In Situ X-ray Spectroscopic Identification and Kinetic Control of Highly Hybridized Co(IV) States in Cobalt Oxide Amorphous Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Valence dynamics of transition metals are central to oxygen evolution reaction (OER) mechanisms, yet in situ spectroscopic studies capturing these dynamics within amorphous catalysts remain limited. Here, we present in situ X-ray spectroscopy of amorphous catalysts, where CoBi exhibits higher OER performance compared to CoPi. While our data shows successive valence changes toward high-valent states in both catalysts, distinct initial electro-structural states dictate the intermediate evolution. Co(III) dominates in both catalysts at open-circuit potential, yet the Co(III)–O–Co(III) bridge structure observed in CoBi is absent in CoPi. Under active OER, Co(IV) species are identified as distinguishable spectral intensities; these are assigned to highly hybridized low-spin (LS) Co(IV) with reduced electron–electron repulsion, as validated by resonant inelastic X-ray spectroscopy (RIXS) analysis of Li0.75CoO2. Density functional theory supports the conversion from tetrahedral (Td) Co(II) to octahedral (Oh) Co(III) and suggests that factors other than thermodynamic pathways are likely responsible for the performance gap. The lower formal oxidation, larger Co–O length, smaller Co–O–Co angle, prominent pre-edge dipole character and absent oxo-bridging in CoPi suggest a kinetically inefficient Co(IV) state. These findings demonstrate that the initial electro-structure strongly influences the formation of productive high-valent active species and the resulting OER activity.

item.title: A Descriptor-Based Approach to Predict the Catalytic Activity of Zinc CO 2 Hydration Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Carbonic anhydrase (CA) catalyzes CO2 hydration with turnover frequencies approaching 106 s–1, but native enzymes lack stability under conditions typical of industrial carbon capture. Small-molecule zinc mimics can be more stable under harsh conditions, but product inhibition by bicarbonate limits efficiency. A general framework for predicting turnover across ligand scaffolds has remained elusive. We report the analysis, by experiment and computation, of speciation and catalytic activity of zinc complexes as CA mimics. A literature data set of twelve Zn-ligand complexes was constructed, and the binding free energy (ΔGbind) of bicarbonate to zinc was calculated by DFT with DLPNO-CCSD(T) refinement. ΔGbind strongly correlates with the intrinsic rate constants of these Zn-ligand complexes for CO2 hydration with R2 = 0.90 at pH 9, 25 °C, and saturated CO2 (1 atm). By comparison, combining the commonly used descriptors ΣE(2), qZn, and %Vburied resulted in R2 = 0.74. Examining additional Zn catalysts (for example, the coordination species [ZnL4(OH)]+, where L is 1-methylimidazole) revealed that chemical speciation must be accounted for to describe the observed dependence of catalytic activity on ligand stoichiometry. Furthermore, accurate ranking of catalytic activity for several of the modified cyclens considered requires accounting for steric congestion (%Vburied), as ΔGbind alone does not capture active-site occlusion. These results define a transferable framework that integrates ΔGbind, speciation, and steric properties to enable the design of Zn-based CO2 hydration catalysts.

item.title: Oxyfunctionalization of Primary Benzylic C(sp 3 )–H Bonds with Water by a Molybdenum-Dependent Dehydrogenase
item.description:
Abstract
The selective oxyfunctionalization of C(sp3)–H bonds remains a central challenge in chemical synthesis. Although oxygenases and peroxygenases provide biocatalytic alternatives to metal-based chemical methods, their practical use is constrained by costly cofactor regeneration, toxic co-substrates, or limited selectivity. Molybdenum (Mo)-dependent alkyl dehydrogenases circumvent these limitations by employing water, rather than O2 or H2O2, as the oxygen source for hydroxylation in conjunction with an electron acceptor. Here, we combine enzymatic, structural, and computational analyses to characterize a Mo-dependent p-cymene dehydrogenase (pCDH) from an anaerobic hydrocarbon-degrading bacterium. Isolated pCDH selectively hydroxylates a variety of benzylic and allylic C(sp3)–H bonds. A 2.0 Å cryo-EM structure of the heterotrimeric enzyme in complex with p-cymene captures key states of the catalytic cycle. Structure-guided QM/MM modelling and docking rationalize the substrate scope and radical mechanism. These results identify water-dependent Mo-dehydrogenases as promising catalysts for selective C(sp3)–H oxyfunctionalization.

item.title: Oriented Charge Flow in a Dual-Active-Site CdS Framework Enables Coupled CO 2 Reduction and Biomass Alcohol Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Solar-driven conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals provides an effective pathway for carbon resource utilization. However, the sluggish kinetics of CO2 reduction and the reliance on sacrificial electron donors limit its practical viability. Herein, we present a bifunctional photocatalyst consisting of spatially separated Ag2S and Au cocatalysts anchored on hollow CdS (Ag2S-Au/CdSH), which enables efficient concurrent CO2 photoreduction to CO and selective oxidation of aryl alcohols to benzaldehyde in a sacrificial-agent-free system. The rational integration of dual-active sites induces oriented charge flow, significantly enhancing photogenerated carrier separation and utilization, as evidenced by ultrafast spectroscopy showing extended electron lifetimes. This synergistic architecture delivers markedly higher production rates of 1.2 mmol g–1 h–1 for CO and 2.5 mmol g–1 h–1 for benzaldehyde, representing approximately 8-fold and 5-fold enhancements over pristine CdS, respectively. Comprehensive in situ spectroscopic studies combined with density functional theory calculations elucidate the distinct roles: Au sites strengthen CO2 adsorption and stabilize intermediates for reduction, while Ag2S promotes alcohol dehydrogenation. This synergistic dual-site architecture maximizes redox efficiency by matching reaction potentials and minimizing carrier recombination. This work provides mechanistic insights into catalyst design for integrated CO2 valorization and biomass upgrading, providing a basis for efficient chemical production.

item.title: Electric-Field-Assisted Oxygen-Vacancy Engineering Promotes Low-Temperature Ammonia Decomposition over Ru/CeO 2 through Interfacial H Migration
item.description:
Abstract
Ammonia decomposition provides a promising route for on-demand hydrogen production, but conventional thermocatalytic systems are constrained by severe kinetic limitations at low temperatures, limiting their compatibility with low-grade heat utilization. Herein, we develop an electric-field-assisted oxygen-vacancy engineering strategy to promote low-temperature NH3 decomposition over Ru/CeO2 catalysts. Ru/CeO2 catalysts with tunable oxygen-vacancy concentrations were prepared via a pre-impregnation and solid-state grinding method. Structural and spectroscopic characterizations reveal that oxygen vacancies intrinsically strengthen Ru–CeO2–x interfacial electronic interactions, promote charge redistribution, and generate relatively electron-enriched Ru sites. More importantly, the applied electric field further amplifies this vacancy-mediated interfacial regulation and facilitates H-species transfer/removal. The optimized Ru/CeO2-OV3 EF catalyst achieves 35.3% NH3 conversion at 150 °C under a high GHSV of 30,000 mL gcat–1 h–1 and exhibits an electric-field-assisted apparent activation energy of only 12.28 kJ mol–1. In situ DRIFTS, TPD measurements, impedance analysis, and DFT calculations collectively suggest that defect-associated O sites near oxygen vacancies provide favorable accommodation sites for migrated H species, while the electric field promotes interfacial polarization and accelerates H transfer from Ru sites to the CeO2–x surface. This synergistic effect reduces H coverage on Ru active centers, regenerates available Ru sites for sustained NH3 activation, and enables stable low-temperature operation. This work clarifies how an external electric field amplifies oxygen-vacancy-mediated interfacial electron/H transfer and provides a rational strategy for efficient low-temperature hydrogen production from ammonia.

item.title: Engineered Asymmetric Ce δ+ -O-P Structures via CeO 2 -CePO 4 Heterojunctions for Continuous Dimethyl Carbonate Synthesis from CO 2 and Methanol
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical fixation of CO2 with CH3OH into value-added chemicals, such as dimethyl carbonate (DMC), plays a crucial role in carbon neutrality and resource recycling. However, its efficiency is limited by the ineffective synergistic activation of CO2 and CH3OH. Here, we employ a strategy to construct CeO2-CePO4 heterojunctions by phosphate-functionalized CeO2, introducing an asymmetric Ceδ+-O-P structure for CO2 and CH3OH activation. The prepared Ce0.8P0.2Oσ catalyst achieves a CH3OH conversion of 28.6% with nearly 100% DMC selectivity and retains its performance for 300 h during continuous DMC synthesis at 140 °C. Experimental characterization supports the formation of local Ceδ+-O-P sites in the catalyst. DFT calculations based on one selected idealized strained model containing a specific local Ceδ+-O-P site show a distinct Bader charge for Ce–O–P and Ce–O–Ce coordinated oxygen atoms within this model. Within the same model, the local Ceδ+-O-P site is associated with elongation of the C–O bond in CH3O* and a lower energy barrier for its dissociation into *CH3 and *O, providing a model-specific interpretation of the enhanced DMC yield. This work develops a design strategy for asymmetric catalytic site via composite oxide heterojunctions engineered for CO2 and CH3OH activation, exhibiting great potential for large-scale continuous CO2 chemical fixation to high-value-added chemicals.

item.title: Promoting Efficient H 2 Dissociation in Photothermal CO 2 Hydrogenation through Functional Separation and Synergistic Coupling of Active Sites
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient H2 dissociation and subsequent spillover of active hydrogen species are critical factors for achieving high activity in CO2 hydrogenation reactions. Herein, we constructed a well-designed and highly dispersed Cu–In bimetallic catalyst supported on CeO2. This catalyst enables the spatial separation of plasmonic enhancement, H2 activation, and CO2 conversion sites, thereby significantly improving H2 dissociation capability and H-spillover efficiency. Comprehensive investigations using multiple transient characterizations, together with in situ/operando spectroscopy, reveal that the three components are tightly coupled through H-spillover, electron transfer, and interfacial interactions. Specifically, the Ce sites on the CeO2 surface serve as the active centers for CO2 conversion via a redox mechanism, while the available indirect but consistent evidence suggests that In species likely act as the primary H2 dissociation sites, promoting the reduction of Cu species and the regeneration of oxygen vacancies on the CeO2 surface through H-spillover. Meanwhile, the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect of Cu significantly enhances the light absorption and photothermal conversion efficiency of the catalyst. The photoexcited LSPR electrons generated by Cu are further transferred to the In species and CeO2 surface, thereby facilitating H2 dissociation and the redox cycling of Ce sites. Such a “functional separation–synergistic enhancement” strategy effectively improves the catalytic activity, and the optimal catalyst achieves a CO yield of 230.1 mmol gcat–1 h–1 W–1 cm2 under 1.5 W cm–2 light irradiation at the surface temperature of 300 °C, significantly outperforming both the corresponding dark reaction and the monometallic Cu/CeO2 and In/CeO2 counterparts. This work provides important design principles and mechanistic insights for constructing highly active CO2 hydrogenation catalytic systems by enhancing H2 dissociation and H-spillover processes.

item.title: Advances in Photothermal CO 2 Hydrogenation to Methane: Mechanistic Insights into Catalytic System Design across Different Scales
item.description:
Abstract
The ever-escalating accumulation of atmospheric CO2 and the growing demand for renewable energy conversion and storage have intensified research into solar-driven CO2 utilization technologies. Photothermal catalytic CO2 hydrogenation to methane has emerged as a promising approach for simultaneous carbon resource recycling and solar energy conversion, synergistically integrating the merits of photocatalysis and thermocatalysis. However, achieving high activity, selectivity, and long-term durability concurrently remains a central challenge, demanding precise control over photothermal conversion efficiency, charge transfer, and mass transport. Rational structural regulation spanning multiple length scales, from individual atoms to clusters, nanoparticles, and macroscopic reactors, is pivotal to overcoming such limitations. This review systematically summarizes research progress from a multiscale catalytic system design perspective, covering single atoms, nanoclusters, nanoparticles, supports, and macroscopic reactors. At each scale, the corresponding structure–activity relationships are analyzed, and the modulation mechanisms of active sites, photothermal effects, charge migration, and mass transport are elaborated. On this basis, we critically evaluate the advantages and bottlenecks of current research and put forward design guidelines and future development directions for next-generation high-performance catalytic systems. This review aims to provide both theoretical insights and practical references for the rational design of advanced photothermal CO2 methanation catalysts.

item.title: Dynamic Change in Oxygen Storage and Release Mechanisms of Pd/CeO 2 –ZrO 2 Catalyst by Isotope Imaging
item.description:
Abstract
Oxygen storage and release on oxygen storage materials such as CeO2–ZrO2 solid solution (CZ) are key phenomena for high-performance automotive three-way catalyst (TWC). In order to clarify the microscopic oxygen dynamics on TWC, oxygen storage distribution in a model catalyst comprising dense CZ substrate with Pd is visualized by combining oxygen isotope labeling and reaction quenching. The effects of temperature, oxygen storage duration, and hydrogen reduction (oxygen release) duration on 18O concentration distribution in the bulk and surface of the model catalysts are systematically investigated. In the temperature range of ≤400 °C, oxygen release and storage originated primarily from the Pd-CZ-gas triple phase boundary (TPB) and Pd surface, while the contribution from the bare CZ surface is limited. Oxygen incorporated from around the TPB diffuses in three directions: toward the CZ depth, CZ surface, and Pd surface. Furthermore, during the oxygen release process, the disappearance of the oxide layer (PdO) on the Pd and the subsequent exposure of metallic Pd accelerate oxygen release from the TPB, expanding the oxygen vacancy region deeper into the CZ directly beneath the Pd. Conversely, in the temperature range of ≥500 °C, in addition to the TPB-mediated process, the oxygen exchange on the entire CZ surface and bulk diffusion are activated, significantly expanding the storage and release regions. This study demonstrates that the OSC (oxygen storage capacity) mechanism in Pd/CZ catalyst is not static; rather, the dominant oxygen release/storage sites and transport pathways dynamically change depending on the temperature and the presence of a PdO layer.

item.title: Local Electric Fields at Organic-Inorganic Hybrid Interfaces Drive Electrocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
The local electric field generated at organic-inorganic hybrid interfaces can profoundly influence electrocatalytic reactions, yet how molecular interfaces regulate local field distributions and reaction pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we combine grand-canonical density functional theory with in situ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy to investigate CO2 reduction at cobalt phthalocyanine-copper (CoPc-Cu) interfaces. Density functional theory calculations show that CoPc creates a confined interfacial microenvironment and modifies the charge distribution at the Cu surface, producing non-uniform local electric fields that are experimentally probed using the vibrational Stark effect of adsorbed CO. Theory and experiment reveal that this field heterogeneity modifies CO adsorption across neighboring Cu sites and increases the adsorption-energy difference between adjacent CO intermediates, thereby lowering the barrier for C–C coupling. Consistent with this mechanism, CoPc-Cu exhibits an enhanced C2+/C1 product ratio, particularly at modest cathodic potentials where the confined hybrid interface is preserved. This work provides direct in situ evidence that organic-inorganic hybrid interfaces can regulate electrocatalytic selectivity through local electric-field engineering, offering design principles for field-enhanced CO2 electroreduction.

item.title: Gold-Catalyzed Chemoselective Dearomative Ring-Opening Modes of Indoles
item.description:
Abstract
A gold-catalyzed dearomative cyclization of indoles with ynone-nitriles assisted by a Lewis or a Brønsted acid has been developed, which provides an efficient route to 4-azafluorenones via an unexpected indole ring-opening process. The key strategy involves the attack of an iminyl intermediate to the indoleninium species at its highly electrophilic C2 position, with both intermediates being generated spontaneously during the dearomatization process. By varying the gold catalyst and acid additives, the 1+1 and 2+1 component reactions can be achieved selectively.

item.title: Restructuring of Cobalt Telluride Electrocatalysts in the Oxygen Evolution Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
Among non-noble metals, transition metal chalcogenide electrocatalysts have high electrocatalytic performance and electrical conductivity, but they experience restructuring in oxidative oxygen evolution reaction (OER) conditions. Unfortunately, it is unknown what triggers such restructuring. In this study, we used cobalt telluride (CoTe) as a model system and combined in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy with ex situ characterizations and DFT calculations to understand the restructuring mechanism. Results suggest that restructuring starts when CoTe is immersed in KOH solution and involves the transformation of Co–Te into Co–O bonds, suggesting that the true OER-active phases derived from CoTe are cobalt oxides or (oxy)hydroxides. The combined data are consistent with restructuring involving Te loss and oxygen incorporation at under-coordinated sites. Leached Te is detected in the electrolyte, while residual oxidized Te-containing species remain associated with the catalyst after restructuring. These observations are consistent with partial Te redeposition and/or retention of Te-containing surface species, which could influence the overall activity. Model-based analysis of the in-situ extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectra and XANES linear combination fitting suggests that the dominant reconstructed phases are Co3O4-like and CoOOH-like species that contribute to OER activity.

item.title: Redox Control of S -Sulfocysteine Formation in Adenosine Phosphosulfate Reductase
item.description:
Abstract
Sulfur assimilation fuels bacterial growth by supplying the reduced sulfur required for the biosynthesis of sulfur-containing biomolecules. Adenosine 5′-phosphosulfate reductase (APSR) catalyzes the reductive step of this pathway, converting adenosine 5′-phosphosulfate (APS) to adenosine monophosphate. This reaction proceeds through nucleophilic attack by catalytic C256, located in the flexible C-terminal tail, on the sulfur atom of APS, forming a thiosulfonate enzyme intermediate. Here, we investigate this reaction in APSR from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an opportunistic pathogen associated with severe infections, particularly in patients with cystic fibrosis. APSR contains an iron–sulfur [4Fe–4S] cluster, which participates in redox steps of the reaction. Here, we show that the redox state of the iron–sulfur cluster also controls the catalytic step. Multiscale molecular simulations investigate how oxidized and reduced cluster states affect APS binding, active site organization, and the nucleophilic attack step. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations show that the oxidized [4Fe–4S]2+ cluster stabilizes substrate interactions and the conformation of the C-terminus, facilitating a catalytically productive orientation of C256. The activation barrier of 17.7 ± 1.7 kcal mol–1 from quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) umbrella sampling MD simulations at the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/6-31G(d) level is consistent with kinetics experiments performed on an ortholog enzyme. The redox state of the iron–sulfur cluster shows its role in modulating the conformation of conserved K144, which is important for transition state stabilization in the nucleophilic attack. These findings illuminate the mechanism of this P. aeruginosa target and provide broader insight into the roles of iron–sulfur clusters in controlling enzyme reactivity.

item.title: Dual Reaction Pathways on Ga 2 O 3 -ZnO/Cu for Efficient CO 2 -to-Methanol Conversion
item.description:
Abstract
The design of metal–support interfaces is critical for overcoming the persistent trade-off between CO2 conversion and methanol selectivity in CO2 hydrogenation. Though an inverse catalyst with an oxide-on-metal configuration provides a platform for tuning interfacial properties, the distinct roles of multi-interfaces with different electronic properties and how they collectively govern reaction pathways remain largely unexplored. Herein, we constructed an inverse Ga2O3-ZnO/Cu catalyst to engineer dual pathways for efficient CO2-to-methanol conversion. Comprehensive characterization reveals that Ga2O3 induces charge redistribution in the catalyst for more oxygen vacancies, which enhance CO2 adsorption. The Cu-ZnO interface facilitates the formation of key intermediates along the formate pathway. Meanwhile, Ga also introduces a RWGS + CO* hydrogenation pathway to preferentially convert CO2 to methanol. In addition, Ga2O3 loading-enabled smaller Cu nanoparticles further enhanced H2 dissociation and spillover on the surface. Consequently, the optimized Ga2O3-ZnO/Cu catalyst achieves a high space time yield of methanol (728.73 gCH3OH kgcat–1 h–1) with a high methanol selectivity of 82.37% at 220 °C and 3 MPa. This work provides insights into engineering reaction pathways for methanol synthesis via the rational design of synergistic active sites.

item.title: Metal-Free Oxidized Carbon Nitride/ l -Proline Synergistic Catalysis: Highly Enantioselective Direct Synthesis of C2-Quaternary Indolinones via Dearomative Oxyalkylation Cascades
item.description:
Abstract
Herein, we report a metal-free, cooperative oxidized graphitic carbon nitride/l-proline catalysis for enantioselective dearomative oxyalkylation of 2-arylindoles. The developed method leverages the band structure of g-C3N4 to efficiently generate singlet oxygen (1O2) under visible light and aerobic conditions, driving an oxidative dearomatization cascade. The resulting intermediates are intercepted via an l-proline-mediated Mannich addition, providing direct access to C2-quaternary indolin-3-ones in high yields (up to 88%) and with enantioselectivities (up to 99% ee). By integrating heterogeneous carbon nitride photocatalysis with asymmetric organocatalysis, this protocol offers a robust, recyclable alternative to traditional noble-metal catalysis for enantioselective synthesis of C2-quaternary indolin-3-ones.

item.title: Copper-Mediated Valence Tautomerism Enables α -C(sp 3 )–H Alkylation of 1,3-Dicarbonyl Compounds and Tryptophans via Photocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Carbonyl α-C(sp3)–H functionalization is a key approach to access functionalized pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and bioactive peptides. Conventional two-electron enol tautomerization strategies for this transformation often suffer from harsh reaction conditions and limited substrate tolerance. While valence tautomerism (VT) enables radical-type C–H activation, such reactivity has been exclusively realized with nickel catalysis, and copper-mediated VT remains unexplored for α-C(sp3)–H activation of carbonyls. Here, we present a dual photoredox/copper catalytic strategy that exploits copper-mediated VT to generate α-carbonyl alkyl radicals. These radicals undergo radical–radical cross-coupling with nucleophilic radicals generated by photocatalytic decarboxylation, delivering α-carbonyl alkylation products. The protocol features mild conditions and broad functional group tolerance, supporting peptide late-stage modification and gram-scale synthesis. Mechanistic studies and density functional theory (DFT) calculations validate a Cu(III)-mediated VT pathway for radical generation. This work establishes copper as a viable VT catalytic platform, expands the scope of dual photoredox/metal catalysis, and offers a versatile tool for biomolecular derivatization.

item.title: Nickel-Catalyzed Regiodivergent and Enantioselective Hydrosilylation of Internal Alkenes
item.description:
Abstract
Enantioselective hydrosilylation of alkenes represents a direct and economical route to chiral organosilanes. However, achieving good regio- and enantioselectivity from the same alkene for the divergent synthesis of chiral silanes remains a formidable challenge, particularly for internal alkenes. In this work, we present a ligand-controlled nickel-catalyzed regiodivergent and enantioselective hydrosilylation of 1,2-disubstituted alkenes. This approach provides a direct access to both α- and β-trifluoromethylsilanes with high regio- and enantioselectivity. The resulting enantioenriched silane products are amenable to various stereospecific transformations. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) calculations elucidate the origin of the observed regio- and enantioselectivity.

item.title: Poly(Ionic Liquid)-Engineered Interfacial Water Reorganization for Selective Acidic CO 2 -to-Formic Acid Electroreduction
item.description:
Abstract
Acidic CO2 electroreduction offers a promising route to improve carbon utilization compared with alkaline or neutral systems. However, maintaining high product selectivity at industrially relevant current densities remains challenging because local CO2 depletion and excessive proton availability intensify the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Herein, we develop a bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3) catalyst modified with a long-chain imidazolium poly(ionic liquid) layer (PIL@BS) for electrocatalytic CO2-to-formic acid conversion at pH 2. In a flow cell containing 3 M KCl, PIL@BS catalyst delivers a high Faradaic efficiency for formic acid (FEFA = 98.4%) at a current density exceeding 300 mA cm–2 and maintains over 80% FEFA after 120 h of continuous operation. Even at low 15 vol % CO2 concentration typical of industrial flue gas, PIL@BS retains higher FA selectivity than unmodified BS, underscoring the effectiveness of PIL in suppressing HER under CO2-limited conditions. Structural characterizations and electrochemical analyses reveal that the PIL backbone creates a hydrophobic interface while preserving CO2 affinity and high ionic conductivity, effectively mitigating the flooding issues and enhancing the local availability of CO2. Operando spectroscopies further show that PIL-regulated interface facilitates access to weakly hydrogen-bonded water. Such interfacial water reorganization disrupts the extended hydrogen-bond network, attenuating the continuous proton-relay pathways that promote the competing HER while maintaining localized proton transfer for CO2 reduction. Combined with theoretical calculations, these findings indicate that the PIL-modified microenvironment enables a direct and energetically favorable hydrogenation pathway toward FA formation. This work highlights the PIL-engineered interfacial microenvironment as a key factor for overriding the intrinsic selectivity of a catalyst and enabling practical CO2 valorization.

item.title: Photoinduced Enantioselective α-Alkylation of Active Methines with Nonactivated Alkenes Using a Chiral Ytterbium Lewis Acid
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic enantioselective alkylation is a fundamental strategy for constructing molecular frameworks bearing chiral carbon centers. Herein, we report a photoinduced highly enantioselective catalytic α-alkylation of active methine compounds with nonactivated alkenes to construct chiral quaternary stereocenters. Cooperative catalysis using an organophotocatalyst and a chiral ytterbium Lewis acid bearing an Indapybox ligand efficiently promotes the alkylation of open-chain 2-substituted β-ketoesters, affording the desired products in high yields with high enantioselectivities (up to 96% yield and 96% ee). The reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope with respect to both the alkene and β-ketoesters components. Furthermore, the resulting products can be readily transformed into optically active 5-pyrazolone and 5-isoxazolone derivatives while maintaining high optical purity.

item.title: Spatially Decoupled Reaction-Diffusion Microenvironments in Mordenite Enable Highly Selective Methane-to-Methanol Conversion
item.description:
Abstract
The selective oxidation of methane to value-added oxygenates represents a formidable challenge in heterogeneous catalysis, fundamentally limited by the thermodynamic trade-off between activating the reactant and preventing the subsequent overoxidation of fragile products. This vulnerability is deeply tied to the spatial accessibility within the catalytic microenvironment; highly open channels, while facilitating mass transfer, indiscriminately expose the generated products to secondary oxidation. Herein, we develop a site-selective construction strategy to establish spatially decoupled reaction-diffusion microenvironments within mordenite (MOR). By utilizing pyridine as a pore-blocking agent to occupy 12-membered ring (12-MR) channels, we preferentially localize the active Cu species, identified as bent mono-μ-oxo dicopper cores, within the well-defined 8-membered ring (8-MR) side pockets. This architecture induces a profound dual spatial effect. At the reaction level, the 8-MR acts as a nanoscopic kinetic shield by providing a customized local topology that suppresses the reactivity of oxygenated intermediates while retaining sufficient methane activation capability. Crucially, at the mass-transfer level, Cu incorporation into the 12-MR main channels is largely suppressed, allowing these channels to serve as unobstructed diffusion pathways and reducing the probability that desorbed methanol recontacts oxidative Cu sites during outward transport. Furthermore, by eliminating the structural heterogeneity inherent to non-selective synthesis, this spatially defined microenvironment and homogeneous Cu coordination structure enable the elucidation of the intrinsic structure-performance relationship. Under continuous operating conditions, this spatially engineered catalyst exhibits high methanol selectivity and productivity, ranking among the leading Cu-MOR systems for methane-to-methanol conversion. These findings demonstrate that designing a decoupled reaction-diffusion microenvironment can regulate catalytic selectivity beyond electronic-structure modulation, while also offering a generalizable method for the site-selective placement of metal ions within zeolite.

item.title: SIFT-MS Enables Product-Specific Insight into Electrochemical Pulsed CO 2 Reduction in Membrane Electrode Assemblies
item.description:
Abstract
Pulsed electrolysis is a promising operating strategy for electrochemical CO2 reduction, but understanding how products form, accumulate, and are released during dynamic operation remains challenging, particularly in membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs). Conventional product analysis methods provide limited time resolution, making them poorly suited for resolving product-specific changes during pulses that are on the timescale of seconds. Here, selected-ion-flow-tube mass spectrometry (SIFT-MS) was used as a quasi-real-time analytical technique to measure the product concentrations during pulsed CO2 electrolysis in a MEA using a copper oxide nanoparticle-derived cathode catalyst. Methodology development for the SIFT-MS technique established the sampling and pulsing criteria required for reliable semi-quantitative analysis of the concentration of reaction products. Applying these methodology developments to pulsed electrolysis experiments unveiled how molecular structure influences product retention within the electrode and subsequent transport into the MEA outlet stream under pulsed CO2R conditions. A comparison of the measured concentrations of ethanol, ethylene, and acetaldehyde provided evidence that the formation of ethanol occurs through multiple contributing reaction pathways. The analysis of the measured concentrations of acetaldehyde, propionaldehyde, and 1-propanol provided evidence for the sequential formation of products through which the formation of aldehydes precedes the formation of 1-propanol. Overall, this work establishes SIFT-MS as a product-specific, quasi-real-time analytical technique for probing pulsed CO2R in membrane electrode assemblies that can unveil crucial information to aid in the development of future MEA electrolyzers and operational strategies.

item.title: Liquid Gallium Nanoislands on Zeolite: A Dynamic Confinement Strategy to Break the Catalytic Trade-Off in Hydrodeoxygenation
item.description:
Abstract
Breaking the pervasive activity–selectivity–stability trade-off in catalytic hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a bifunctional nanoisland catalyst (GaNPs-Pt/Beta) that overcomes this limitation by utilizing liquid gallium nanodroplets anchored on Beta zeolite as mobile nanoislands. These islands effectively restrict platinum single-atom migration and agglomeration. Concurrently, Brønsted acid sites provided by the zeolite sea facilitate the dehydration-etherification process. This synergy enables highly efficient transfer hydrogenation at the gallium–platinum interface, achieving selective C–O bond cleavage while preserving C═C bonds under mild conditions. Benefiting from this island-sea architecture, the GaNPs-Pt/Beta catalyst delivers high catalytic activity, achieving >99% cinnamyl alcohol conversion and 93.8% β-methylstyrene selectivity within 6 h at 160 °C, with recyclability demonstrated over nine cycles involving intercycle regeneration. This strategy is scalable to diverse α,β-unsaturated aldehyde/alcohol chemicals, demonstrating that zeolite-based liquid metal nanoislands provide a versatile platform for the sustainable synthesis of high-value chemicals.

item.title: Adsorbate Site Hopping—More Facts and Fiction: Driving Forces and Relevance for Heterogeneous Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Adsorbate site hopping, defined here as surface-confined migration of adsorbed species or adsorbate equivalents between distinct sites, is a widespread phenomenon in heterogeneous catalysis and includes spillover between different surface phases. Because it enables communication between spatially separated functionalities, site hopping has often been viewed as a route to bifunctional catalytic synergy and, in some cases, to performance beyond constraints imposed by Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi relationships. However, its catalytic value is conditional rather than universal. Downhill migration to a stronger binding site may increase local barriers for subsequent transformation or introduce site-regeneration penalties, while kinetically accessible hopping may remain irrelevant if it does not reduce the energetic span of the catalytic cycle. In addition, apparent rate enhancements assigned to site hopping can arise from other modes of intersite communication, including desorption–readsorption, subsurface or bulk diffusion, ion–electron intersite coupling, catalyst restructuring, or changes in active-site identity. This Perspective develops a thermodynamic and kinetic framework for distinguishing these processes and assessing when site hopping becomes catalytically consequential. We discuss driving forces, hopping barriers, coverage and dynamic surface effects, kinetic signatures, and diagnostic pitfalls, with the aim of clarifying when site hopping can be used as a catalyst design principle.

item.title: Diastereodivergent Synthesis of 8,12-Guaianolides Using Engineered P450 BM3
item.description:
Abstract
8,12-Guaianolides are a class of sesquiterpene lactones that exhibit diverse biological activities, which are often strongly influenced by structural variations, including the stereochemistry of the C8 oxygen substituent. Here, we report a concise, diastereodivergent approach to both 8α,12- and 8β,12-guaianolide scaffolds from santonin-derived triene 5 by combining engineered cytochrome P450 BM3-catalyzed allylic C–H hydroxylation with a photochemical rearrangement. The P450 BM3 mutant LG-23 selectively hydroxylates the C8α position of 5, whereas a single additional mutation, L437I, inverts the facial selectivity to favor C8β hydroxylation. Structure-guided mutagenesis and docking studies suggest that the β-methyl group of Ile437 remodels the active site and enforces a flipped substrate binding mode that directs the opposite C8 C–H bond toward the heme iron. The utility of this enzymatic stereochemical switch was demonstrated by the synthesis of the 8α,12-guaianolides xerantholide (1) and mikanokryptin (2) and the 8β,12-guaianolide 11,13-dehydroachalensolide (4). This study demonstrates that a single active-site mutation in P450 BM3 can switch the facial selectivity of C–H hydroxylation at one carbon center, providing a strategy for stereodivergent enzymatic oxidation in complex-molecule synthesis.

item.title: Influence of Extraframework Metal Species on the Kinetics and Spatial Distribution of Coke during Methanol-to-Hydrocarbons Conversion over ZSM-5 Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
The incorporation of selected extraframework cations is a common approach to tuning the performance of zeolite catalysts in industrially relevant methanol-to-hydrocarbons (MTH) conversion processes, although the mechanistic origin of their effects remains incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the relationships between MTH and coking kinetics, the nature and distribution of coke deposits, and the positions of extraframework calcium and zinc species in the ZSM-5 catalyst, which promote alkene and aromatic formation, respectively. At comparable Brønsted acid site densities, enhanced aromatics formation over zinc-containing ZSM-5 is accompanied by a 2× higher intrinsic MTH activity and a 150× faster active site loss than over the calcium-containing catalyst. Photoelectron photoion coincidence spectroscopy shows that faster coke-forming kinetics over the zinc-containing catalyst is linked to enhanced formaldehyde formation via methanol dehydrogenation, triggering a cascade of intermediates, such as dienes and aromatics, a pathway inhibited in the calcium-containing catalyst. This also leads to a higher fraction of high-molecular-weight coke in the zinc-containing catalyst and a predominance of surface graphitic coke in the calcium-containing catalyst, as revealed by complementary thermogravimetric, microscopic, and spectroscopic analyses. Powder neutron diffraction indicates that coke preferentially occupies the channel intersections and extends along the straight channels in both catalysts. However, the average coke orientation differs as calcium-containing ZSM-5 comprises more distorted intrapore aromatic deposits, whereas zinc-containing ZSM-5 accommodates more planar aromatic coke. The confinement of coke in micropores is consistent with the preferential location of cations determined by high-resolution X-ray diffraction analysis, which shows that calcium occupies two sites in the sinusoidal channels, with one of these pointing toward the channel intersections, whereas the smaller zinc-associated density is found at sites in five- and six-membered rings between main channels, at the expense of occupancy of sinusoidal channel-based positions. Consequently, faster coke-forming kinetics linked to the dehydrogenation activity of extraframework zinc species, together with lower spatial strain at channel intersections, favor the formation of more condensed, planar-like coke in zinc-containing catalysts. Conversely, the larger size and higher channel occupancy of calcium sites destabilize aromatics and hinder coke formation in this key intersecting zone. These results show that extraframework species influence not only the reaction kinetics but also the local organization and orientation of confined coke, in part through steric constraints associated with their crystallographic location.

item.title: Rhodium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Hydroformylation of Vinyl Ethers as a Key Step in the Synthesis of Chiral Fine Chemicals
item.description:
Abstract
The rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric hydroformylation (AHF) of vinyl ethers provides a powerful synthetic step to yield chiral aldehydes as products or intermediates for industrially relevant fine chemicals. Out of the 40 chiral ligands tested, the phosphine-phosphorodiamidite (S,S,RP,S)-BettiPhos L7 and the phosphine-phosphoramidite ligand L6 performed best in this transformation, combining high activity, regio- and enantioselectivity. Branched 2-aryloxypropionaldehydes (16 examples) were obtained with b/l-ratios ranging from 3.1:1 to exclusive branched products, and with enantioselectivities between 79 and 94% ee. Interestingly, for these substrates, the selective decomposition of the linear aldehydes to the respective arenols and acrolein via β-hydride elimination was observed. Branched 2-alkyloxypropionaldehydes (3 examples) were obtained with fair b/l-ratios (1.7:1–2.6:1) and good to high enantioselectivities (85–95% ee). The utility of this transformation was demonstrated by synthesizing the commercial herbicide (R)-Mecoprop on a gram scale in 69% yield and 91% ee via hydroformylation of 4-chloro-2-methyl-1-(vinyloxy)benzene, followed by oxidation. The catalytic system could also be used under slightly modified reaction conditions for reductive asymmetric hydroformylation to produce in one-pot chiral 2-aryloxypropanols. The synthetic potential was further explored by applying the tandem asymmetric hydrohydrazonemethylation (AHHM) followed by reduction, yielding γ-chiral N′-substituted acetohydrazides as shown for 6 examples. Hydrogenolysis of the crude product mixtures results in the corresponding chiral primary amines, as demonstrated in the synthesis of 2-phenoxypropanamine from (vinyloxy)benzene with an overall yield of 74% and 94% ee on a gram scale. Moreover, another tandem reaction—specifically, the asymmetric hydrosulfiniminomethylation (AHSM)—enables access to halogen-containing chiral primary amines, as demonstrated by the synthesis of 2-(4-chlorophenoxy)propanamine in an overall yield of 53% and >99% ee.

item.title: Extremely High Turnover Number and Turnover Frequency of an Iron Chlorin Complex for Photocatalytic Water Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Highly active water oxidation catalysts based on earth-abundant elements are strongly demanded for practical application of artificial photosynthesis. An iron complex with a chlorin ligand derived from chlorophyll-a demonstrated the highest turnover frequency (= 21.3 ± 0.3 s–1) and turnover number (= 6920 ± 110) among homogeneous catalysts reported for photocatalytic water oxidation utilizing [RuII(bpy)3]2+ (bpy: 2,2′-bipyridine) and S2O82– as a photosensitizer and a sacrificial electron acceptor, respectively. The molecular nature of the Fe chlorin complex during the photocatalytic water oxidation was confirmed by dynamic light scattering analysis and electrospray ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry. Also, kinetic studies suggested that the rate-determining step is O–O bond formation via coupling of two high-valent iron–oxo species formed by three-electron oxidation of the mononuclear Fe chlorin unit with water. The high planarity of the chlorin ligand enables the high-valent iron–oxo species to approach another iron–oxo unit closely, thereby facilitating O–O bond formation.

item.title: Achieving Ordered-Cationic-Vacancy-Mediated Photohole Transfer Dynamics via Phase and Facet Engineering toward Highly Efficient Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting
item.description:
Abstract
Defect engineering is promising to solve the photocarrier dynamics mismatch between rapid bulk recombination and sluggish surface oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in PEC water splitting but is limited by forming random or bulk defects. Herein, we adopt a phase and facet modulation strategy to construct a 2D defective spinel β-In2S3 photoanode with highly exposed, well-ordered indium vacancies (VIn). These VIn introduce a shallow acceptor level near the valence band (VB), which induces selective photohole capture to VIn shallow traps. The efficient and fast (∼0.13 ps) photohole transfer from the VB to the VIn state and the sharply elongated lifetime for photoholes accumulated at VIn, by facilitating band-edge exciton dissociation, induce separation efficiency nearly 100% even at low bias. Meanwhile, surface VIn lowers the OER barrier by boosting the conversion of *OH to *O and promotes surface reaction kinetics, enabling the photohole transfer efficiency to reach 95%. Thus, VIn simultaneously acts as photohole-capture centers and surface-active sites to optimize photohole separation and interfacial transfer dynamics. Through introducing and exposing ordered VIn to reaction interfaces, the β-In2S3-2D photoanode achieves a record-high photocurrent density of 9.7 mA cm–2 at 1.23 VRHE and an IPCE reaching 80% without hole scavengers. Such a regulation mechanism can guide reverse design of defective semiconductor photoanodes for efficient PEC conversion.

item.title: Gold(I)-Catalyzed Asymmetric Transformations of 1-(1-Alkynyl)cyclobutyl Ketones: Access to Enantioenriched Cyclopenta[ b ]furans Bearing Vicinal Bridged Quaternary Stereocenters
item.description:
Abstract
Present herein is a gold(I)-catalyzed asymmetric cascade reaction of 1-(1-alkynyl)cyclobutyl ketones. Upon activation by a chiral phosphoric-acid-tethered gold(I) complex, they undertake intramolecular 5-endo-dig cyclization, and the resulting oxocarbenium species engage in an asymmetric 1,2-alkyl migration to generate gold-containing cyclopenta[b]furan carbocations, which can be intercepted by a broad range of nucleophiles, including indoles, pyrroles, alcohols, and amines, providing efficient access to synthetically challenging tetrahydro-4H-cyclopenta[b]furans bearing vicinal bridged quaternary stereocenters with fair to high enantioselectivity. The intermediates can also participate in (3 + 2) annulations with suitable 1,3-dipoles to afford polycyclic architectures with high molecular complexity. Mechanistic studies and density function theory calculations elucidate the key factors governing the catalytic pathways and stereochemical outcomes.

item.title: Direct Amidination of Alkenes Via C–H Activation of Pyridinyl Formimidamide Synthon
item.description:
Abstract
Alkenes are among the most abundant and versatile feedstocks in synthetic chemistry, yet methods for their direct and regioselective conversion into nitrogen-containing frameworks remain scarce. In particular, the direct catalytic amidination of alkenes has remained underdeveloped. Herein, we report a rhodium-catalyzed anti-Markovnikov amidination of alkenes using a stable pyridinyl formimidamide synthon. This reaction enables the direct installation of amidine moieties onto a wide range of alkenes, including styrenes, aliphatic alkenes, and challenging internal alkenes that undergo efficient chain-walking with high regioselectivity and broad functional group tolerance, accommodating unprotected amines, phenols, and halides. The resulting pyridyl amidines can be readily transformed into amides, carboxylic acids and esters, establishing a practical platform for alkene diversification. Notably, late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules, including cyclosporine A, FK506, and quinine etc., provides access to previously inaccessible analogues. Mechanistic investigations, highlighted by the crystallographic capture of a key rhodium–aminopyridinyl formimidamide intermediate, provide compelling evidence for the proposed catalytic cycle. Collectively, this work not only fills a critical gap in alkene functionalization but also offers a concise and general route to high-value nitrogen-containing architectures.

item.title: A Curvature-Induced Pentagonal Oxide Motif Governs Ethylene Epoxidation Selectivity on Silver Nanoparticles
item.description:
Abstract
Silver-catalyzed ethylene epoxidation is a cornerstone of the chemical industry, yet the operando surface structure of Ag nanoparticles and the identity of selectivity-governing active sites remain elusive. Here, we integrate machine learning potentials, stochastic surface walking global optimization, molecular dynamics simulation, and statistical analysis to resolve the surface landscape of Ag nanoparticles approaching experimentally relevant sizes under reaction conditions. Oxygen-induced reconstruction transforms pristine Ag facets into a globally amorphous oxide layer composed of three types of locally ordered ring motifs interspersed with structural defects. A pentagonal motif (ring5), topologically required to accommodate nanoparticle curvature and absent in conventional slab models, dominates the surface across all investigated particle sizes. Its recessed central Ag atom acts as an electronic charge buffer that weakens the critical C–Ag bond in the oxametallacycle intermediate, conferring high intrinsic ethylene oxide selectivity. Microkinetic analyses confirm that the oxygen species of ring5 regulate ethylene oxide yield, peaking at a nanoparticle oxidation degree of O/Ag ≈ 0.3–0.4. This work establishes a statistical paradigm for decoding active phases on realistic catalyst surfaces through dynamic structural ensembles.

item.title: Plasma-Enabled Direct Methane-to-Methanol Conversion on Zeolite-Confined Copper-Oxo Clusters: Insight into Vibrational Excitation and Radical-Mediated Process
item.description:
Abstract
Selective one-step conversion of methane (CH4) to methanol (CH3OH) remains a grand challenge in catalysis, constrained by the trade-off between C─H bond activation and product overoxidation. Here, we integrate density functional theory (DFT) calculations with plasma-catalytic experiments to investigate direct CH4-to-CH3OH conversion using H2O as the sole oxidant on CuxOy clusters within MOR zeolite, compared to the CuO(111) surface. We show that C─H bond activation proceeds preferentially via homolytic H-abstraction on zeolite-confined CuxOy clusters, with Cu3O3/MOR exhibiting a low activation barrier of only 0.21 eV, more than three times lower than that on CuO(111). Vibrational mode-specificity analysis shows that the C─H stretching modes couple most effectively on higher-barrier surfaces. Importantly, we demonstrate that plasma-generated radical intermediates (CH3·, H·, OH·) reshape the reaction thermodynamics, with the Gibbs free energy shifting from endothermic (+1.13 eV) to exothermic (–3.21 eV and –8.25 eV), enabling pathways inaccessible under thermal conditions. Experimentally, Cu/MOR catalysts prepared by ion exchange, which favor well-dispersed zeolite-confined Cu-oxo sites, achieve the highest CH3OH production rate (0.26 mmol/h) at low plasma power (6.5 W), outperforming catalysts prepared by wetness impregnation. This work bridges Cu-oxo site topology, vibrational mode specificity, and radical-mediated thermodynamics, offering valuable insights for plasma-catalytic selective CH4-to-CH3OH conversion.

item.title: Multiobjective Optimization of Synthetically Accessible Homogeneous Catalysts Reveals Tradeoffs for Methane-to-Methanol Conversion
item.description:
Abstract
The selective conversion of methane to methanol remains a major challenge in catalysis, and no earth-abundant homogeneous catalyst has been demonstrated to carry out this transformation with high turnover. To explore previously synthesized complexes that might be amenable for this transformation, we start from macrocyclic ligands from experimental structures in the Cambridge Structural Database. After expanding this set of ligands with Hammett-tuning functionalization, we construct a design space of 21.9 million Mn and Fe catalysts. We employ active learning using neural network surrogate models with quantified uncertainty to efficiently identify catalysts with optimal methane-to-methanol turnover. We do this by jointly optimizing density functional theory (DFT)-computed hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and methyl radical rebound energetics. Square planar tetraaza-based macrocycles in combination with low-spin Fe(II) or Mn(II) emerge as a privileged class of transition metal complexes within the Pareto-optimal set, with Mn(II) catalysts exhibiting balanced energetic tradeoffs of the two steps. In contrast, porphyrin catalysts exhibit favorable HAT but unfavorable rebound, and seesaw catalysts, which are not widely employed, are indeed the least favorable in our set. Full reaction coordinate analysis of representative Pareto-optimal catalysts reveals that HAT and rebound thermodynamics no longer govern turnover, which is instead determined by the stability of the metal–oxo intermediate and the rebound kinetic barrier. Nonetheless, the resulting energetic spans for these catalysts remain competitive with known earth-abundant, methane-to-methanol catalysts, underscoring the effectiveness of active learning for discovering previously unexplored, synthetically accessible catalysts and unraveling catalyst design principles for methane-to-methanol reactivity.

item.title: Nickel-Catalyzed Enantioselective Cyclizative Alkylation of 1,6-Enynes with Diazo Compounds and Alkyl Halides
item.description:
Abstract
Transition-metal-catalyzed cyclization of 1,n-enynes represents a versatile platform for the construction of structurally diverse chiral heterocycles. Despite substantial advances in this field, the enantioselective cyclizative alkylation of 1,n-enynes remains a formidable synthetic challenge, primarily due to the inherent difficulty in simultaneous control of regio-, chemo-, and stereoselectivity. Herein, we disclose a highly enantioselective cyclizative alkylation of 1,6-enynes employing two complementary alkylating reagents: diazo compounds and readily available alkyl iodides. This protocol proceeds under mild conditions and features broad substrate scope, delivering enantioenriched γ-lactams and pyrrolidine derivatives bearing quaternary stereogenic centers in good yields (up to 81%) and enantioselectivities (53 examples, up to 98% ee). Mechanistic studies corroborate that these two types of alkylating reagents follow entirely distinct catalytic pathways.

item.title: Chemoenzymatic Cascade Recycling and Upcycling of Polyurethane Elastomers
item.description:
Abstract
The complex structure of polyurethanes (PURs) presents a major barrier to their efficient recycling. Here, we report a chemoenzymatic cascade that enables the simultaneous recycling and upcycling of PUR through rapid alkaline pretreatment followed by urethanase-catalyzed depolymerization. Using in-house-synthesized model polyether- and polyester-based PUR elastomers, we establish that soft-segment chemistry dictates the composition, morphology, and accessibility of the pretreated residues, thereby governing the efficiency of the subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis. This insight enabled translation of the cascade to a commercial PUR elastomer, achieving >93% chemical conversion and recovery of up to 1 mM 4,4′-methylenedianiline (MDA) (97.2% purity), corresponding to a 40-fold increase over the nonenzymatic control, together with polyols obtained in 95% isolated yield that were directly reused for PUR synthesis. Mechanistic studies further show that alkaline pretreatment enhances substrate accessibility for the enzyme, and structural analysis of urethanase SP2 reveals a carbamate-specific hydrogen-bonding interaction that promotes urethane hydrolysis while minimizing esterase activity. The cascade was additionally applied to highly crosslinked commercial PUR foams and adhesives, demonstrating its versatility toward industrially relevant waste streams. Overall, this work establishes a mechanistically informed chemoenzymatic platform for PUR depolymerization and provides a strategy for converting chemically recalcitrant PUR waste into reusable molecular building blocks.

item.title: Entropy-Enhanced Catalysis Accelerates Low-Temperature CO 2 Methanation via Intermediate Delocalization at Under-Coordinated Ru 2+ − V O Sites
item.description:
Abstract
In heterogeneous catalysis, the electronic structures of catalysts' active sites are modified to optimize intermediate binding and bond activation for achieving high reaction activity. However, studies on regulating the atomic structures of catalytic materials to enhance the configurational diversity of adsorbed intermediates remain scarce. Herein, we demonstrate that engineering under-coordinated active site motifs enables an entropy-enhanced catalytic mechanism that harnesses the configurational freedom of surface intermediates to improve reaction rates at reduced temperatures. Using CO2 methanation as a model reaction, we identified that under-coordinated Ru2+−oxygen vacancy (Ru2+−VO) sites promote delocalized catalyst−intermediate interactions and reduce the reaction energy barrier. Stable Ru2+−VO sites were created on Au nanoparticle-grafted (RuOx)a(CeOy)b solid-solution nanorods through plasmonic effects under reducing conditions. Eyring plot analysis revealed an activation entropy gain of TΔΔS‡ ≈ 12 kJ mol−1 for CO2 methanation at 300 °C, in situ spectroscopy revealed a *HCOO-mediated pathway, and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations indicated a 0.22 eV free-energy barrier for *HCOO formation on Ru2+−VO motifs. A CH4 production rate of 550 mmol gcat−1 h−1 with >98% selectivity and >280 h stability at 300 °C was achieved at a high gas hourly space velocity of 40,000−100,000 mL gcat−1 h−1. The findings provide a conceptual framework beyond adsorption energy optimization in catalyst design, showing that configurational entropy is a tunable descriptor for enhancing catalytic kinetics.

item.title: Dual-Enzyme Relay Catalysis Enables Asymmetric Construction of Nonadjacent Stereocenters in Polycyclic Alcohols
item.description:
Abstract
The asymmetric construction of nonadjacent stereocenters in a single catalytic system remains a significant challenge due to the difficulty in controlling stereochemical relay between sequential transformations. Herein, we report a dual-enzyme relay catalytic system that integrates an artificial streptavidin-based copper metalloenzyme (Sav-Cu) with an engineered ketoreductase (KRED) for the one-pot synthesis of polycyclic alcohols bearing 1,3-non-adjacent stereocenters. In this relay process, the engineered SavDMase variant (S112A/K121D) catalyzes a non-natural decarboxylative Mannich reaction to establish the R-configured stereocenter in the enantioenriched ketone intermediate, which is then recognized by the engineered KREDAV mutant (S96A/Y190V) and reduced with high diastereo- and enantioselectivity to install the S-configured alcohol stereocenter, thereby furnishing the (R,S)-configured product as the dominant stereoisomer. The optimized system furnishes the products in up to 83% yield, 99% ee, and 96% de across a broad substrate scope, and is readily applicable to 2 mmol-scale synthesis. Structural analysis, docking, and molecular dynamics simulations support complementary roles of the two catalytic modules: SavDMase promotes productive organization of the Mannich step, while KREDAV stabilizes the reactive binding pose and constrains the hydride-transfer trajectory to enforce stereoselective reduction. This work demonstrates how artificial and natural enzymes can be integrated in relay catalysis to solve challenging stereochemical relay problems beyond the reach of individual biocatalysts.

item.title: Repurposing a Donor 2-OH Group for Catalyst-Controlled Stereodivergent Glycosylation
item.description:
Abstract
The free C2-OH group of glycosyl donors is generally viewed as a liability in glycosylation because it can act as a competing nucleophile and compromise stereocontrol. Here, we show that this functionality can instead be harnessed as a programmable stereochemical element in a catalyst-controlled stereodivergent glycosylation. A single β-configured 2-hydroxy glycosyl 8-alkynyl-1-naphthoate donor was found to deliver either β- or α-glycosides simply by changing the gold(I) catalyst system. Triflate-based catalysts promoted highly β-selective glycosylation, whereas bistriflimide-based conditions enabled complementary α-selective glycosylation from the same donor. The method is applicable to a range of carbohydrate and noncarbohydrate acceptors and enables the programmable assembly of glucooligosaccharides bearing β-(1→6), α-(1→6), and alternating α/β-(1→6) linkages from a common donor platform. Mechanistic studies, including intermediate characterization, variable-temperature NMR experiments, computational analysis, and control glycosylations with the corresponding 2-O-Bn donor, reveal distinct roles of the donor 2-OH group in the two stereochemical manifolds.

item.title: The Two Opposite Faces of Ceria as Redox Mediator in Methane Dry Reforming
item.description:
Abstract
We investigate the interplay between carbon accumulation and redox-driven deactivation pathways in cerium-containing nickel (NiCe) and palladium (PdCe) bimetallic precursor materials upon eventual decomposition into a Ni- or Pd-ceria interfacial system during dry reforming of methane (DRM). By probing defined intermediate states, information from surface electronic structure, morphology, and bulk structure to track structural and chemical changes across several reaction, deactivation, and CO2 titration cycles is combined to identify how carbon accumulation, oxygen transfer, and dynamic metal–ceria interfacial interactions evolve under DRM reaction conditions. Despite their similar cerium-containing precursor architecture and surface composition, the two systems allow studying two detrimental deactivation processes. Bimetallic NiCe decomposes more readily into a Ni-ceria interface, where carbon formation is progressively suppressed. Loss of activity is a result of oxidation of Ni particles mediated by enhanced oxygen transfer from ceria. In contrast, bimetallic PdCe is much more decomposition-resistant, and the localized Pd-ceria interface exhibits high activity throughout multiple DRM cycles, even in the presence of substantial carbon deposition and filamentous carbon growth. The results demonstrate an intrinsic coupling between carbon accumulation and oxygen transfer to the metallic component, with carbon acting as a competing sink for reactive oxygen species. We emphasize the significance of dynamic interfacial structures and show that ceria-mediated oxygen transfer produces contrasting, metal-dependent catalytic outcomes. Whereas in NiCe, efficient oxygen delivery suppresses carbon accumulation, but progressively oxidizes Ni and diminishes methane activation, in PdCe, carbon generation outpaces oxygen-mediated removal, yielding a carbon-rich yet catalytically persistent surface.

item.title: Solar-Driven Highly Active and Selective Conversion of Acetonitrile to Formic Acid over Oxygen Vacancy Engineered Tungsten Oxide
item.description:
Abstract
Photocatalytic activation of inert chemical bonds represents a promising route for selective conversion of organic molecules such as acetonitrile (CH3CN) into value-added products. However, as the most common reactive oxygen species, •OH radicals are nonselective and usually lead to overoxidation reactions, making it difficult to realize the target product with both high activity and selectivity in the photocatalytic system. Here, we demonstrate that, through oxygen vacancy (Vo) engineering, selective CH3CN conversion into HCOOH is enabled over a WO3 photocatalyst under mild conditions. Under simulated solar irradiation, the as-prepared Vo-rich WO3 nanosheets display notable photocatalytic CH3CN conversion performance, with a HCOOH yield rate of 8.8 mmol g–1 h–1 and a selectivity as high as 86.5%. In combination of various in situ spectroscopic techniques, it is revealed that the Vo constructs a coupling match between of •OH radicals and •CH2CN intermediates on the WO3 photocatalyst surface, which facilitates the selective conversion of CH3CN into HCOOH while preventing its overoxidation. This work extends the conversion pathway of CH3CN in a photocatalytic route and provides deeper insight into the selective conversion of inert molecules.

item.title: Lewis–Brønsted Dual-Acid Sites Induced H-Down Interfacial Water Configuration and Accelerated Proton Transfer toward Enhanced Acidic Oxygen Evolution
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient activation of interfacial water molecules and fast proton transfer are critical but challenging for the acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Herein, a Lewis–Brønsted dual-acid catalyst design strategy is proposed to achieve accelerated acidic OER by synergistically optimizing the configuration of interfacial water molecules and proton transfer kinetics on Mn-doped IrO2. In this catalyst, the Mn dopant serves as a Lewis acid site that readily captures hydroxyl groups, which perturbs the local hydrogen-bonding network and induces interfacial water molecules to form an H-down configuration toward surface active sites, thereby promoting the enrichment and dissociation of reactive interfacial water. On this basis, the formation of the Mn–Obri–Ir local structure enhances the Brønsted acidity of the bridge oxygen (Obri) site, accelerates the deprotonation of the Obri–H bond, promotes the formation of key OER intermediates and accelerates the reaction kinetics. Mn dopant also induces electron enrichment around Ir, suppresses excessive oxidation and dissolution of Ir species, and enhances catalyst stability performance. These synergistic effects enable Mn-IrO2 to achieve a 160 mV overpotential at 10 mA cm–2 and to operate stably for 1500 h at 10 mA cm–2 and 1200 h at 1.0 A cm–2 in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), demonstrating the promising potential of the Lewis–Brønsted dual-acid strategy in acidic OER catalyst design.

item.title: Reductive Dispersion of In 2 O 3 into H-CHA and Reversible Formation of Isolated In(I)/In(III) Species under H 2 /O 2 Redox Cycling
item.description:
Abstract
The reductive dispersion of metal oxides into isolated cationic species in zeolites is an important strategy for generating well-defined catalytic sites, yet its kinetics and molecular mechanism remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate the H2-induced redispersion of In2O3 physically mixed with H-CHA using in situ/operando UV–vis spectroscopy, In K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), SEM-EDS mapping, modulation-excitation spectroscopy, H2-TPR, XRF, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Time-resolved UV–vis spectroscopy quantitatively tracks the consumption of bulk-like In2O3 under H2 and reveals that the redispersion rate depends on temperature, H2 concentration, In2O3 precursor properties, and zeolite framework. Higher temperatures and H2 concentrations accelerate the process, with the highest reliable initial rate observed at 600 °C under 10% H2. In K-edge XANES indicates selective formation of reduced In species assigned to framework-stabilized In+ rather than metallic In0, demonstrating a partial-reduction pathway in CHA. H2-TPR provides quantitative redox evidence consistent with reductive solid-state ion exchange and reversible reduction of isolated oxygen-containing In species. SEM–EDS mapping shows the disappearance of surface In-rich domains after H2 treatment, consistent with indium redistribution, while XANES provides bulk-sensitive evidence for formation of reduced In species. Operando redox-cycling experiments reveal reversible interconversion between In(I) and oxygen-containing In(III) species under H2/O2 switching. DFT calculations using representative 1Al and 2Al CHA models suggest that local Al environments can influence the relative stability of framework-bound reduced In(I) and oxygen/hydroxyl-containing In(III)-type species. Together, these results support a two-step mechanism in which bulk In2O3 is first reduced to mobile In+ species and then anchored at acid sites within the zeolite framework. This work provides mechanistic insight into reductive redispersion and offers design principles for regenerable indium-based zeolite catalysts.

item.title: Deep-Learning-Driven Discovery and Engineering of Imine Reductase for the Efficient Synthesis of Chiral Opine Derivatives
item.description:
Abstract
The narrow amine donor scope of imine reductases (IREDs) limits their application in the synthesis of opine compounds. Herein, we report a machine learning (ML)-guided protein engineering strategy to address this limitation. An IRED from an unclassified Ensifer, IRED5, was identified through deep-learning-based screening for its strict enantioselectivity toward methyl glycinate. Subsequent engineering using a few-shot learning for protein fitness prediction approach yielded the M178T/A208L/P241V/A36E/S67Q/Q187N (M6) variant with six mutations across the active site and protein surface. Kinetic analysis showed 156-fold toward methyl pyruvate and 72-fold improvements toward methyl glycinate in catalytic efficiency, respectively, over the wild-type (WT) enzyme. M6 accepted diverse keto esters and amino acid esters, enabling stereoselective formation of opine derivatives bearing two stereocenters. Structural and computational analyses revealed the molecular basis for activity enhancement. In preparative synthesis, M6 achieved complete conversion at a 3 M substrate loading, corresponding to a space time yield of 366 g·L–1·d–1. At a 4 M substrate loading, conversion remained high at 95.4% with a space time yield of 525 g·L–1·d–1, affording 10.5 g of enantiopure methyl N-(2-methoxy-2-oxoethyl)-d-alaninate (1a) in 75.0% isolated yield with > 99.9% ee. This work establishes an efficient biocatalytic route to opine compounds and demonstrates the utility of ML-guided enzyme engineering in expanding IRED synthetic capability.

item.title: Synergy of Ni Nanoparticles and MoO x Species for Selective Hydrodeoxygenation of Lignin into Cycloalkanes
item.description:
Abstract
The selective hydrodeoxygenation of lignin as a substitute for fossil resources into aviation fuel-range cycloalkanes faces significant challenges due to its complex structure and diverse reaction pathways. Herein, we introduced MoOx species onto Ni nanoparticles-loaded Beta zeolite (Ni-0.2MoOx/Beta), which catalyzed the complete hydrodeoxygenation of lignin dimers and lignin-derived phenols into the corresponding cycloalkanes under mild conditions (200 °C, 2 MPa H2). Ni-0.2MoOx/Beta also enabled the hydrodeoxygenation of real lignin, achieving a cycloalkanes selectivity of over 83%. Mechanistic studies indicated that the synergistic effect between Ni nanoparticles and MoOx species was key to enhancing the hydrodeoxygenation performance. Ni nanoparticles enabled the adsorption and dissociation of H2, and horizontally adsorbed benzene ring in the oxygen-containing substrate, while adjacent MoOx species with abundant oxygen vacancies facilitated the vertical adsorption of oxygen-containing groups in the ring-saturated intermediates and the activation of C–O bonds. Simultaneously, the strong hydrogen spillover on Ni-0.2MoOx/Beta ensured the benzene ring hydrogenation and the cleavage of C–O bonds. This work provides an approach for designing non-noble metal catalysts for lignin hydrodeoxygenation, holding significant value for advancing the application of lignin-based aviation fuels.

item.title: Diastereoselective Heterogeneous Hydrogenation of Fused Arenes Directed by Amines and Alcohols
item.description:
Abstract
The heterogeneous hydrogenation of aromatic compounds using supported metal catalysts is an efficient strategy to increase the three-dimensionality and molecular complexity of organic molecules. However, most heterogeneous hydrogenation methods lack stereoselectivity or rely upon the steric properties of the substrate for stereocontrol, which limit their predictability and generality for pharmaceutical synthesis applications. In this work, we develop two synthetic methods for the amine- and hydroxyl-directed hydrogenation of benzofused arenes using Rh/C and Pt3Cu/SiO2 as heterogeneous catalysts, respectively. Mechanistic studies on the amine-directed reaction reveal that simultaneous adsorption of the amine and benzene functional groups to the Rh metal surface is extremely strong, outcompeting the adsorption of the benzene or amine individually and enabling good turnover and high diastereoselectivity toward the amine-directed product. A broad scope of benzofused scaffolds are effective substrates, generating up to four stereocenters in a single step. The utility of the method is demonstrated in the synthesis of a pyridine bisoxazoline compound derived from perhydro-cis-aminoindanol.

item.title: High-Density Iridium Single Atoms on Vanadium-Doped TiO 2 for Electrochemical Water Oxidation Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Water oxidation in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) uses IrO2 nanoparticles supported on corrosion-resistant TiO2. However, the low conductivity of TiO2 imposes electronic transport limitations that necessitate high Ir loadings for effective catalysis. Here, we present a catalyst design strategy that couples a heavily V-doped TiO2 support with high-density Ir single atoms, enabling water oxidation at minimal Ir loading. In this design, Ti-site-substituted V provides n-type doping, and selective V leaching creates cation vacancies that anchor Ir as isolated atoms. TEM with convolutional neural network (CNN)-based analysis shows Ir single-atom density increases with V content, accompanied by lower charge-transfer resistance and higher Ir-specific activity. The density functional theory indicates that cation-site Ir introduces a midgap state below V 3d levels and shifts neighboring V 3d orbitals toward the Fermi level. Ir1/V-TiO2 achieves 1480 A gIr–1 at 1.55 V vs RHE (1.3 wt % Ir) and demonstrates device-level PEMWE operation at an Ir loading as low as 0.027 mgIr cm–2.

item.title: Catalytic Asymmetric Allylic Substitution with Alkynylogous Silyl Enol Ethers En Route to Chiral Allenes
item.description:
Abstract
Despite their potential as building blocks of allenes, alkynylogous enol silanes have rarely been employed in organic synthesis. Herein, we establish their utility as nucleophiles in catalytic asymmetric allylic substitution, which results in skipped enallenes bearing two vicinal stereogenic elements (axial and central chirality). This iridium-catalyzed reaction utilizes α-alkynyl silyl enol ethers as alkynylogous nucleophile for reaction with easily accessible racemic branched allylic alcohols and endows tetrasubstituted axially chiral allenones, bearing a δ-stereocenter exclusively as a single regioisomer in moderate to good diastereoselectivity (up to 11:1 dr) and in most cases with high enantioselectivity (up to >99.5:0.5 er). The densely functionalized γ-allylic allenones can be elaborated into useful building blocks, including a highly substituted chiral 2-allyl furan derivative. Through this work, α-alkynyl enol silanes are introduced as alkynylogous nucleophiles in transition metal catalysis.

item.title: Tailoring Dynamic Cu Redox Responsiveness via Pr-Modified Ceria for Enhanced Reverse Water–Gas Shift
item.description:
Abstract
The reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reaction is a key technology for converting CO2 into CO as a versatile intermediate for chemical production. Among various catalysts, Cu/CeO2 has attracted considerable attention owing to its high CO selectivity, yet its activity is affected by the oxidation and reduction behavior of Cu under reaction conditions. Although rare-earth modification has been widely employed to improve the redox properties of ceria, the relationship between support modification and the dynamic Cu redox behavior during RWGS remains poorly understood. Herein, we demonstrate that Pr modification effectively tailors the Cu redox response of Cu/CeO2, leading to enhanced RWGS performance. Systematic comparison of lanthanide modified ceria supports revealed that Pr-modified CeO2 exhibited the highest catalytic activity while maintaining approximately 99% CO selectivity. Comprehensive structural characterization combined with in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy showed no major difference in the surface species detected after Pr modification. Instead, the Pr-modified Cu/CeO2 catalyst exhibited a faster oxidation response under CO2 together with reversible reduction under an H2 atmosphere. The enhanced Cu redox dynamics are associated with the modified redox characteristics of the Pr-modified CeO2 support. These results identify dynamic Cu redox responsiveness as an important characteristic associated with the enhanced RWGS activity of the Pr-modified Cu/CeO2 catalyst and provide a practical strategy for engineering reducible oxide-supported Cu catalysts for efficient CO2 conversion.

item.title: Metal-Dependent Control of Methoxy Retention versus Cleavage in Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation of Lignin-Derived Aromatics
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemical hydrogenation of lignin-derived aromatics offers a route to biomass upgrading, but controlling methoxy retention versus cleavage remains challenging. Here, we compare carbon-supported Rh, Pt, Ru, and Pd catalysts for guaiacol conversion under identical conditions. Rh/C and Pt/C are the most active catalysts but favor sharply different pathways: Rh/C promotes methoxy-retaining ring hydrogenation, whereas Pt/C preferentially forms demethoxylated products. Time-resolved profiles, intermediate-feeding experiments, and initial-rate analysis indicate that this selectivity difference emerges predominantly during early reaction branching. The apparent activation free energies of methoxy retention and demethoxylation are closely matched on Rh/C (91.1 and 91.8 kJ mol–1, respectively), but favor demethoxylation on Pt/C (91.1 and 89.2 kJ mol–1, respectively). Calculations on model surfaces suggest that metal-dependent interactions with adsorbed guaiacol facilitate access to different bond-activation pathways, providing a possible molecular basis for the observed kinetic preference.
