The Rh/Pt selectivity contrast persists across the investigated potentials and temperatures and extends to four additional lignin-derived aromatics as a broader difference in functional-group retention and cleavage. These results link metal-dependent early pathway partitioning to control over oxygen retention in electrochemical biomass upgrading.

item.title: Chiral Phosphoric Acid-Catalyzed Asymmetric Allylic Dearomatization of Tryptamines with Alkoxyallenes
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic asymmetric dearomatization of tryptamines has emerged as a powerful strategy for constructing chiral pyrroloindoline frameworks, which are ubiquitous in bioactive natural products. Despite tremendous advances in transition-metal-catalyzed synthesis of allyl-substituted pyrroloindolines, organocatalytic approaches remain elusive. Herein, we report a chiral phosphoric acid-catalyzed asymmetric allylic dearomatization of tryptamines with alkoxyallenes. This protocol features mild conditions and a broad substrate scope, delivering chiral pyrroloindolines in good yields (up to 93% yield) with stereoselectivity (up to >19:1 E/Z, 99% ee). Mechanistic studies suggest that a covalent adduct forms between the alkoxyallene and the chiral phosphoric acid. This catalytic system demonstrates a transformation of alkoxyallenes and offers a metal-free approach to access enantioenriched allyl-substituted pyrroloindolines, with significant potential for the synthesis of structurally diverse alkaloids.

item.title: Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry for Characterization of Ir-Based Catalysts for PEM Water Electrolyzers
item.description:
Abstract
Iridium-based catalysts remain essential for enabling durable oxygen evolution in proton-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), yet their surface and subsurface chemistries remain insufficiently resolved by conventional characterization methods. Here, we establish time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS), combined with multivariate analysis, as a framework for deconvoluting chemical-, structural-, and depth-dependent features across commercial IrOx powders spanning amorphous and rutile phases. Static and Ar cluster-sputtered ToF-SIMS spectra reveal distinct surface hydroxylation, oxide fragment distributions, and subsurface chemical signatures that differentiate amorphous and rutile IrOx and expose synthesis-dependent residues. Across all powders, surface regions are enriched in hydroxylated IrOx fragments, while subsurface regions show increased reduced Ir species and carbon-based ions. ToF-SIMS fragments are correlated with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) extracted parameters, providing complementary surface chemical information that supports species identification. Finally, integrating ToF-SIMS and XPS descriptors with electrochemical and structural metrics yields a chemically resolved picture linking hydration depth, oxidation state distribution, and structural order to catalytic behavior. This multi-technique, multivariate framework provides insight into the chemical features governing Ir-based OER performance and supports the rational design of robust, efficient catalysts.

item.title: Lewis Acid-Catalyzed Vinyl Transfer Using Vinylene Carbonate for Direct Synthesis of C2,C3-Unsubstituted Indoles
item.description:
Abstract
C2,C3-unsubstituted indoles are privileged scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, yet their direct assembly from simple C2 feedstocks remains a longstanding synthetic challenge. Herein, we report an example of Y(OTf)3-catalyzed C–H [3 + 2] annulation of anilines with vinylene carbonate, enabling direct access to structurally diverse parent indoles through a Lewis acid-catalyzed vinyl-transfer process. Readily available vinylene carbonate serves dually as a C2 building block and an internal oxidant, allowing the reaction to proceed without directing groups, external oxidants, or preinstalled unsaturation while exhibiting broad functional-group compatibility. Mechanistic studies reveal a bifunctional catalytic role of Y(OTf)3 in sequential N-formylmethylation and electrophilic cyclization. This work establishes a distinct strategy for bulk chemical-based indole synthesis and provides opportunities for Lewis acid-catalyzed vinyl transfer chemistry.

item.title: Photoenzymatic Enantioselective [2+2] Cycloaddition of Alkynes Enabled by Whole-Cell Directed Evolution
item.description:
Abstract
Enantioselective excited-state photocycloadditions represent an attractive yet challenging strategy for accessing optically active strained molecules. Here, we report a whole-cell directed evolution platform for engineering artificial triplet photoenzymes that catalyze the enantioselective [2 + 2] photocycloaddition of alkynes. By employing calcium chloride-mediated membrane permeabilization, we overcome substrate accessibility limitations in whole-cell systems and enable high-throughput evolution without the need for cell lysates or purified enzymes. Through ten rounds of directed evolution, a primitive ancestor (APC1.0; 46% yield, 6% ee) was transformed into a highly efficient variant (APC10.0; 92% yield, 94% ee under whole-cell conditions; 99% yield, 97% ee as the purified enzyme). The enhanced activity of APC10.0 enabled a total turnover number of 1800. This work establishes a generalizable strategy for the evolution of artificial photoenzymes and expands the scope of biocatalysis toward stereoselective excited-state transformations.

item.title: Deep-Red Photocatalysis via Charge-Transfer Excitation of a Dicationic Ru(II) Sensitizer Using 740 nm Light
item.description:
Abstract
We report rare examples of deep-red Ru(II) photochemistry from a charge-transfer (CT) excited state using [Ru(bpy)2(p-biphe)](PF6)2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine; p-biphe = 6,6′,7,7′-biphenanthridine). The absorption of deep-red light (740 nm) generates a dark but reactive CT excited state that can be harnessed in proof-of-principle reductive and oxidative electron-transfer and energy-transfer photocatalysis.

item.title: Quantified Structure–Performance Relationships for Fe(III)K(I) Heterodinuclear Catalysts in Cyclohexene Oxide/CO 2 Ring-Opening Copolymerization
item.description:
Abstract
Catalyst design and understanding are improved by quantified structure–performance relationships, but these are underutilized in polymerization catalysis. In epoxide/carbon dioxide ring-opening copolymerization (ROCOP), an important route to make polymers from bio- and waste-based feedstocks, significant success has been achieved in understanding cobalt catalysts, but understanding of other metal catalysts is much less developed. This work targets earth-abundant bimetallic catalysts featuring iron and potassium. A series of seven Fe(III)K(I) catalysts, coordinated by different ancillary ligands, are compared with analogues Co(III)K(I) catalysts; the iron catalysts demonstrate both high activity (TOF = 675 h–1) and polymer selectivity (98%) in cyclohexene oxide/carbon dioxide copolymerization (20 bar CO2 pressure, 100 °C). The Fe(III)K(I) catalysts also show a linear free energy relationship between the copolymerization rates and the catalyst ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) wavelength, with a volcano relationship identifying the best catalysts. The most active catalysts have an Fe(III) center with an intermediate LMCT wavelength, and these features are consistent with the proposed copolymerization mechanism. In this field of catalysis, quantified structure-performance relationships are very rare; thus, the findings are fundamentally interesting and should help to accelerate the design of better-performing iron-based polymerization catalysts.

item.title: Insertion of Alkenes into Aryl Nitrile C–C Bonds Enabled by Thiophenolate Photocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Insertion of alkenes into chemical bonds represents a powerful strategy for carbon framework editing, yet direct insertion into C–C bonds remains a formidable challenge due to the nonpolarity, high-lying σ* orbital, steric shielding, and high thermodynamic stability of the C–C bond. Here, we present a visible-light-driven thiophenolate photocatalytic system that enables direct insertion of alkenes into the C–C bond of aryl nitriles. Mechanistic studies reveal a photoinduced single-electron transfer from the excited thiophenolate anion to the aryl nitrile, generating a radical pair that undergoes radical addition and radical–radical cross-coupling, followed by elimination and nucleophilic addition to afford the insertion product. This strategy not only provides an avenue for editing inert C–C bonds but also establishes thiophenolate photocatalysis as a platform for challenging bond constructions under transition-metal-free and redox-neutral conditions.

item.title: Computationally Guided Design of Facet-Defined Multielement Active Sites on Hexagonal Close-Packed High-Entropy-Alloy Nanosheets for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
item.description:
Abstract
Nonconventional hexagonal close-packed (HCP) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide distinct catalytic surfaces, but their synthesis with well-defined facets remains challenging, leaving facet-dependent multielement ensemble effects largely unexplored. Here, we report the computationally guided realization of atomically thin RuRhIrPtPd HEA nanosheets with predominantly exposed HCP {001} facets for the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations identify HCP {001} as the most favorable facet over {100} and {110}, where near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption, narrow energy distribution, and balanced hydrogen/hydroxyl binding create an optimized alkaline HER landscape. Guided by this prediction, RuRhIrPtPd HEA atomic layers are epitaxially grown on HCP Ru nanosheets to maximize {001} exposure, with atomic-resolution electron microscopy and synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) confirming atomically mixed HEA layers. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the {001}-faceted HEA nanosheets exhibit higher alkaline HER activity and durability than irregular-faceted nanocrystal counterparts and commercial Pt/C. Climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations, operando XAS, and CO-stripping measurements identify Ru-centered ensembles as favorable Volmer sites, showing the lowest water-dissociation barrier of 1.04 eV compared with 1.13–1.47 eV for other metal sites, while neighboring multimetallic sites balance hydrogen and hydroxyl adsorption. This work provides a structural blueprint for harnessing facet-defined multielement ensembles to design high-entropy electrocatalysts.

item.title: Untangling the Molecular Mechanism of SpCas9 HNH Domain Checkpoint Activation: A Gear-and-Wedge Fitting Model
item.description:
Abstract
The CRISPR-associated endonuclease Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) facilitates site-specific DNA cleavage, with structural transition from the checkpoint state to the catalytic conformation representing a critical activation step. This transition involves an approximately 38 Å displacement of the HNH domain catalytic residue H840 toward the target DNA. However, the molecular determinants governing this large-scale rearrangement of the HNH domain during checkpoint activation, and the conformational routes by which HNH repositioning may occur, remain incompletely understood. To address this knowledge gap, we combined nudged elastic band-guided sampling with unbiased molecular dynamics simulations, reaching a cumulative timescale of 160 μs, and constructed a kinetic model describing HNH domain dynamics during checkpoint activation with Markov state modeling. The mechanistic features suggested by these simulations were further evaluated through biochemical DNA cleavage assays and an intracellular fluorescence reporter system. Our results identify conformational plasticity of the L2 linker and coupled motion of the REC2 domain as key regulatory elements of the HNH domain relocation during SpCas9 checkpoint activation. The model suggests that L2 linker remodels toward a disassembled state to enable release and repositioning of the HNH domain, while the REC2 domain outward displacement guides HNH domain relocation through transient interactions that stabilize activation-associated intermediates. Site-directed mutagenesis of key residues in the L2 linker and REC2 domain significantly reduced DNA cleavage efficiency in both biochemical and cellular assays, supporting their functional importance in SpCas9 activation. Taken together, this study provides an experimentally grounded mechanistic framework for understanding how linker dynamics and REC2 domain coupling regulate HNH domain checkpoint activation, and offers insights for rational engineering of SpCas9 variants with altered activity and specificity.

item.title: Titanium-Catalyzed Divergent Deoxycyclization for Synthesizing Semisaturated Nitrogen Heterocycles
item.description:
Abstract
Semisaturated nitrogen heterocycles, such as 3-pyrrolines and unsaturated azepanes, possess highly prized three-dimensional geometries for drug discovery. However, their divergent synthesis from simple, unactivated feedstocks remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a highly selective, titanium-catalyzed divergent radical deoxycyclization coupling of nitrosoarenes and 1,3-dienes. Following an initial aza-Diels–Alder cycloaddition, an in situ generated low-valent titanium(III) species mediates single-electron homolytic cleavage of the robust oxazine N–O bond, yielding a transient nitrogen-centered aminyl radical. By rationally tuning the solvent coordination sphere and chlorosilane dissociation kinetics, this radical’s trajectory is selectively directed down two orthogonal pathways: a 5-exo-tet cyclization to afford 3-pyrrolines (formal [4 + 1]) and a highly strained vinylaziridine-mediated aza-Claisen rearrangement to yield unsaturated azepanes (formal [4 + 3]). This radical-polar crossover protocol features broad functional group tolerance and enables a streamlined, cyanide-free synthesis of the antiarrhythmic drug candidate SU-13197. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including EPR spin-trapping, support the crucial aminyl radical intermediacy and the important role of titanium coordination in orchestrating cascade divergence.

item.title: Coordination-Controlled Stability of Pd Single-Atom Catalysts under Electrochemical Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
Single-atom catalysts (SACs) maximize atom utilization and site-specificity for diverse chemical and electrochemical transformations. While activity and selectivity have been optimized through advanced synthetic methods, the electrochemical stability of SACs remains insufficiently understood and limits practical application. Here, we employ operando inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to quantify the dissolution kinetics of palladium (Pd) SACs in acidic electrolyte across a wide potential window. Operando electrochemically coupled mass spectrometry (EC-MS) confirms concurrent carbon support corrosion. By systematically varying heteroatom dopants, applied potentials, electrolyte pH, and adsorbing anions, we decouple coordination-driven (intrinsic) and electrochemical (extrinsic) factors controlling metal leaching. Specifically, the external potential exhibits a more pronounced influence on the stability of Pd SACs, while the coordinating heteroatoms modulate stability through both direct interaction with the isolated Pd centers and influence on the carbon support. Complementary X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveal dynamic restructuring of the Pd coordination environment, linking local chemical structure to macroscopic stability. These results provide mechanistic insights into SAC degradation pathways and establish design principles for stable single-atom architectures in energy conversion applications.

item.title: Understanding the Role of Band Bending and Surface Coordination in Steering Piezocatalytic In Situ H 2 O 2 Evolution Routes
item.description:
Abstract
Piezocatalytic H2O2 production, employing water and oxygen as the raw materials, is emerging as a promising and viable alternative for in situ H2O2 evolution. However, the understanding of the structure–activity relationship of piezocatalysts still poses challenges, and the key factor steering the H2O2 evolution pathway also remains ambiguous. Herein, two bismuth ferrite-based materials with different crystal structures, perovskite-type BiFeO3 and mullite-type Bi2Fe4O9, were prepared for a systematic comparison of their piezocatalytic activity and an in-depth investigation into the routes of H2O2 in situ production. As a result, BiFeO3 achieved a higher H2O2 production rate (252.86 μmol·L–1) than Bi2Fe4O9 (140.32 μmol·L–1) over 60 min in ambient aqueous conditions without any sacrificial agent. Mechanism analysis reveals that a higher piezocatalytic H2O2 yield of BiFeO3 arises from its stronger piezoelectric response and surface coordination mode of bridging hydroxyl groups. The piezoelectric-induced band bending made water oxidation thermodynamically feasible, and the bridging hydroxyl groups offered hole-transfer channels, thereby collectively triggering the simultaneous occurrence of oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and water oxidation reaction (WOR). This work provides fundamental insights into the crystal-structure-dependent piezocatalytic activity, offering a profound understanding of the mechanism underlying H2O2 evolution routes.

item.title: Spatial Separation of Metal–MOF Tuning Catalytic Selectivity in CO 2 Hydrogenation and Methanol Partial Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Tuning the interactions between metal nanoparticles (NPs) and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is pivotal for selective catalysis, yet systematic regulation of metal–MOF spatial separation remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that systematically regulating the metal–MOF separation enables controlled modulation of catalytic activity and reaction selectivity. A series of MOF-encapsulated Pt catalysts with adjusted Pt–MOF separations were designed and synthesized by varying the surface coverage of capping agents on Pt NPs. Both CO2 hydrogenation and methanol partial oxidation exhibit volcano-type dependencies of catalytic performance on Pt–MOF separation, revealing the existence of an optimal spatial window for catalytic cooperation between Pt NPs and MOF nodes. Theoretical calculations indicate that an appropriate Pt–MOF separation facilitates the formation of key reaction intermediates, thereby governing catalytic selectivity. This work establishes metal–MOF spatial separation as an important structural parameter for catalyst design and provides a practical strategy for developing proximity-engineered NP–MOF catalysts with tunable reaction selectivity.

item.title: Structural and Mechanistic Insight into Oxidative Ring Opening Catalyzed by L-DOPA Extradiol Dioxygenase from Beta vulgaris
item.description:
Abstract
Betalain pigments replace anthocyanins in the majority of plants from the order Caryophyllales, but they are also present in some fungi and bacteria. Their biosynthesis attracts considerable scientific interest due to their applications across various fields and also because plant pigmentation is used to study complex evolution within Caryophyllales. The key step in betalain biosynthesis is the oxidative ring opening of L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-DOPA) catalyzed by L-DOPA extradiol dioxygenase (DODA, EC: 1.13.11.29), which yields 4,5-seco-DOPA; the latter cyclizes to betalamic acid, the chromophore of all betalains. Betalain-producing plants feature two to six homologues of DODA, yet only one of them is highly active and participates in the betalain biosynthesis. Here, we report the crystal structures of the highly active DODAα1 from Beta vulgaris (beetroot), the main commercial source of betalain pigments. High-resolution structures of the apo form and complexes with L-DOPA and three substrate analogues (4-nitrocatechol, 6-nitro-L-DOPA, mimosine) provide insights into the key interactions responsible for effective substrate recognition by the enzyme. Enzymatic reaction kinetics for WT BvDODAα1 show that the enzyme is three orders of magnitude more efficient than the previously studied homologue BvDODAα2, with a pH optimum of 6.5, and that the kinetics are affected by modest substrate inhibition. The residues selected based on X-ray structures for site-directed mutagenesis, except Asp81, are critical for efficient catalysis, whereas molecular dynamics simulations show that they form strong direct and through-water contacts with the L-DOPA amino acid side chain. Mössbauer spectroscopy, supported by DFT calculations, suggests that the catechol ring of L-DOPA binds to the enzyme with both hydroxyl groups unionized, yet upon coordination to Fe2+, one of its protons is transferred to a second-shell histidine. EPR spectroscopy of NO adducts suggests that both L-DOPA and NO can bind simultaneously to Fe2+ in the active site. Based on these experimental data, a cluster model of the Michaelis complex was constructed and used in DFT investigations of the key steps of the enzymatic reaction, which reproduce the observed reaction regiospecificity and provide clues on how this regiospecificity is achieved. Comparison of the BvDODAα1-L-DOPA complex to other experimental structures of ES complexes of extradiol dioxygenases highlights the catalytic role of the distal “proton-shuttle” histidine.

item.title: Divergent Kinetics and Rate-Determining Steps for 1-Butene and 2-Butene Hydroformylation with a Bidentate Phosphoramidite Ligand: A Combined Experimental and Density Functional Theory Study
item.description:
Abstract
The hydroformylation of mixed butenes (1-butene and 2-butene) to n-valeraldehyde is an important industrial process, yet the distinct kinetic behaviors of the two isomers under identical catalytic conditions remain insufficiently understood. Herein, a comprehensive kinetic and mechanistic investigation of 1-butene and 2-butene was conducted using a robust, water- and air-stable, highly regioselective bidentate phosphoramidite ligand-modified rhodium catalyst in a homogeneous system. Systematic kinetic experiments revealed that the hydroformylation of 2-butene exhibits a strong positive dependence on H2 pressure and obvious substrate inhibition at high concentrations, whereas 1-butene shows little H2 dependence and no substrate inhibition. Using a semi-empirical hyperbolic kinetic modeling, the rate equations capture these distinct behaviors with high accuracy (R2 = 0.9746 for 2-butene, 0.9642 for 1-butene). Kinetic studies revealed distinct rate behaviors for 1-butene and 2-butene hydroformylation. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations on the n-valeraldehyde pathway further showed that hydride insertion to the internal C═C double bond has the highest barrier for 2-butene, while CO insertion to the linear rhodium n-butyl intermediate has the highest barrier for 1-butene, providing the mechanistic origin for the observed kinetic differences. The iso-valeraldehyde pathway is additionally disfavored by a 2.7 kcal·mol–1 higher RDS barrier, consistent with the good n-selectivity. In situ high-pressure FTIR spectroscopy further confirmed the five-coordinate hydride HRh(CO)2(P)2 as the catalyst resting state. These findings offer quantitative guidance for optimizing industrial hydroformylation processes using mixed butene feedstocks.

item.title: Engineering a Proton-Regulating Interfacial Microenvironment for Durable RuO 2 Electrocatalysis in PEM Water Electrolysis
item.description:
Abstract
Proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis is a technology for hydrogen production, but its deployment is limited by the cost and durability of acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts. RuO2 exhibits intrinsic OER activity yet degrades rapidly under high-current-density operation and start–stop cycles. Sluggish interfacial proton dissipation may contribute to this instability by promoting proton accumulation and local acidification. Here, we report an atomic-level microenvironment engineering strategy via aliovalent strontium incorporation into rutile RuO2. Modified RuO2 features a structurally distorted and electronically polarized interface that, according to calculations, alters interfacial water organization and may favor oxygen-end-oriented water configurations near the Sr-modified regions. This modified interfacial environment is associated with alleviated local acidification, facilitated proton-transfer-related processes, suppressed lattice oxygen participation, and favored surface-confined oxygen coupling. Operando characterization in a PEM membrane–electrode assembly further supports dynamic interfacial water reorganization and enhanced proton-transfer kinetics under device-relevant conditions. Modified RuO2 delivers 10 mA cm–2 at 197 mV in acidic electrolyte and, in a PEM electrolyzer, achieves 1 A cm–2 at 1.686 V, operates for over 400 h with Ru dissolution suppressed to 5.79 ng h–1, and withstands 3102 start–stop cycles. These findings support interfacial microenvironment regulation as a strategy for improving the durability of Ru-based acidic OER catalysts.

item.title: Nano-CeO 2 -Derived BaCeO 3– x N y H z : A High-Purity Oxynitride-Hydride Support for Enhanced Ammonia Synthesis
item.description:
Abstract
Hetero-anion doping has emerged as an effective approach to modulate the physicochemical and catalytic properties of perovskite-type oxides. In this study, nanosized CeO2 synthesized by a continuous flow-type supercritical hydrothermal synthesis (SHS) process was employed as a precursor for a solid-state reaction with Ba(NH2)2, enabling the low-temperature synthesis of single-phase perovskite oxynitride–hydride BaCeO3–xNyHz (BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS) with a high surface area and abundant N3– and H– species. Ru-loaded BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS exhibited a maximum ammonia synthesis rate of 9.0 mmol g–1 h–1 at 300 °C and 0.9 MPa and showed up to a 6-fold enhancement in activity compared with the corresponding Ru/BaCeO3–xNyHz prepared from commercial CeO2, owing to the enhanced generation of anion vacancies at the Ru–support interface. Moreover, BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS acted as a highly efficient support for various transition metals in ammonia synthesis and for Ni in ammonia decomposition, achieving >99% conversion at 560 °C with a low apparent activation energy (75 kJ mol–1). These findings demonstrate that enhancing the solid-state reactivity of oxide precursors through nanoscale engineering provides a general strategy for the low-temperature synthesis of highly active hetero-anion perovskite catalysts for ammonia synthesis and decomposition.

item.title: Boosting Ethanol Production via Strategic CO Co-Feeding in CO 2 Hydrogenation over Rh-Based Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
The catalytic hydrogenation of carbon dioxide (CO2) to ethanol is a highly promising reaction for carbon utilization and the production of renewable fuels and chemicals. Achieving high ethanol selectivity remains the biggest challenge in the field. Ethanol formation on rhodium (Rh)-based catalysts from CO2 hydrogenation relies on the carbon monoxide (CO) insertion pathway that is kinetically limited compared to the competing hydrogenation of methyl intermediates to methane. In this study, we demonstrate that adding CO to the CO2 hydrogenation reaction stream over colloidally synthesized Rh/Fe/Li–TiO2 catalysts can effectively overcome this limitation. This direct co-feeding strategy promotes C–C coupling and suppresses methanation, increasing ethanol selectivity 5-fold to 24% and boosting the space-time yield 6-fold with only a 15% CO cofeed (CO/(CO + CO2)). Under optimized, hydrogen-deficient conditions (H2/(CO + CO2)), the ethanol selectivity further increases to 32%. Our findings present an efficient, simplified pathway for upgrading CO2-rich streams into higher-value chemicals.

item.title: Enantioselective Alcohol Oxidation Reactions Catalyzed by Unspecific Peroxygenases
item.description:
Abstract
The enantioselective oxidation of alcohols can be achieved via kinetic resolution of racemic alcohols or the desymmetrization of meso-diols. Biocatalytic alcohol oxidation approaches are known, using alcohol dehydrogenases and copper-and flavin-dependent oxidases, but the application of unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) to enantioselective alcohol oxidation has received very little attention. As part of ongoing research into the catalytic promiscuity of UPOs, we present three distinct enantioselective biocatalytic alcohol oxidation approaches: the UPO-catalyzed oxidation of meso-diols via desymmetrization, the chemoselective oxidation of nonbenzylic sites in unsymmetrical diols, and the kinetic resolution of axially chiral biaryl alcohols. In each of the three reaction classes, the isolation of enantiomerically enriched oxidized products is demonstrated on a preparative scale.

item.title: A Redox-Switchable Framework Bridges Dilute-Stream CO 2 Capture and Conversion
item.description:
Abstract
Integrating CO2 capture from dilute sources with electrochemical conversion could bypass the energy-intensive separation and regeneration required in conventional carbon capture and utilization. Yet combining these functions, particularly for multicarbon electrosynthesis, remains challenging. Here, we report an ion-regulated conjugated pyridine-imine framework (Cr-PyN) that performs both electrochemical CO2 capture and selective conversion to acetate within a single metal-free molecular platform through potential-dependent molecular reactivity. Reduction activates the pyridine-imine unit for CO2 binding, while Na+ coordination within the crown cavity regulates the interfacial environment and suppresses hydrogen evolution. Cr-PyN captures CO2 directly from simulated flue gas (9.3% CO2, 3% O2) with an electron utilization efficiency of 0.98 and a minimum electrical energy requirement of 39 kJ mol–1 CO2. At more cathodic potentials in an aqueous flow electrolyzer, the same molecular framework selectively produces acetate with 71% Faradaic efficiency at –0.4 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode and remains stable over 120 h. Complementary in situ and ex situ spectroscopic studies, including operando FTIR and NMR, along with DFT calculations, support CO2 binding and subsequent reaction pathways toward multicarbon conversion.

item.title: d -Electron Descriptors for Nitrate Reduction Reaction Activity in Co-Based Heusler Phase Electrocatalysts
item.description:
Abstract
The tunability of electronic structure in intermetallics opens the door to systematic studies in catalysis. Here, we experimentally investigate various descriptors for the electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction using 9 Heusler phases as catalysts (Co2VSn, Co2MnAl, Co2MnGe, Co2MnSn, Co2FeGe, Co2MnSb, Ni2MnSn, Co2FeSi, and Co2FeAl). In contrast to previous studies with Co-based Heusler phases and oxide perovskites for OER, we find that generally, the total valence electron count, rather than eg filling, provides a better prediction of the activity. However, with period 5 Y elements, such as Sn and Sb, at high valence electron counts, Y-site d-band centers must also be considered. Reaction mechanism analysis by DFT also clarifies the role of X/Y sites. Hence, a single descriptor alone is not sufficient to rationalize catalytic activity across the full spectrum of Heusler phase compositions. So far, valence electron control has relied on single metal or binary alloy compositions for nitrate reduction; however, these Heusler phases help decouple the element identity and valence count while also serving as a guide for more catalysts based on ternary intermetallics. This work thus establishes multi-descriptor guidance for a wide group of catalyst compositions that were previously relatively unexplored.

item.title: Bifunctional Bi-OOH Motifs for Oxygen-Promoted CO 2 Photoreduction via Inhibition of Oxygen Reduction
item.description:
Abstract
Photocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction from practical gas sources is often severely compromised by the competitive O2 reduction reaction. Herein, we report an approach to switch O2 from a competitor into a promoter by arresting the oxygen reduction reaction pathway at the *OOH intermediate stage on BiOBr photocatalysts. The introduction of oxygen vacancies (VO) facilitates O2 reduction to *OOH, which is robustly anchored by VO-induced Lewis acidic Bi sites to form stable Bi-OOH motifs. The Bi-OOH motifs arrest further oxygen reduction pathways and preferentially adsorb CO2 to stabilize *COOH intermediates. A clear linear correlation between the VO concentration and the activity further verifies the vital role of these sites. The BiOBr-VO-0.7 photocatalyst with an optimized VO concentration achieves a 3.4-fold enhancement under 20% O2 (69.2 μmol g–1 h–1) and a 2.9-fold enhancement under simulated flue gas compared to anaerobic conditions for CO2 reduction to CO. Isotope-labeling experiments with 13C confirmed that the CO originated from CO2 reduction. Its practical viability is further demonstrated under natural sunlight and ambient air with a CO generation rate of 5.6 μmol g–1 h–1. This work provides a paradigm shift in the design of catalysts that can use real CO2 sources.

item.title: Sequential Oxygen Vacancy Formation Governs Cu Size-Dependent Methanol Synthesis at Cu–ZrO 2 Interfaces
item.description:
Abstract
Methanol synthesis at Cu–ZrO2 interfaces requires CO2 activation, H2 dissociation, and conversion of oxygenated intermediates to proceed in concert, yet how Cu aggregation coordinates these functions remains unclear. Electronic-structure calculations, molecular dynamics, and catalytic experiments show that Cu size governs sequential oxygen vacancy formation and the adsorption landscape of HCOO*. Isolated Cu atoms favor formation of the initial vacancy and lower the HCOO* formation barrier to 17.41 kcal mol–1, consistent with high methanol selectivity and the highest apparent turnover frequency at 240 °C. When a second vacancy is introduced near isolated Cu in the calculation, HCOO* adsorption strengthens by 31.41 kcal mol–1 and creates a deep thermodynamic trap. Cu clusters instead change HCOO* adsorption by only 4.66 kcal mol–1 as the second vacancy forms and couple bidentate CO2 activation at the vacancy with H2 dissociation on adjacent Cu atoms. This balanced interface gives the highest CO2 conversion and methanol space–time yield of 562.90 mgMeOH gcat–1 h–1 at 280 °C and remains stable for 100 h. Cu nanoparticles, despite their higher Cu loading, interact weakly with CO2 and have the highest HCOO* formation barrier of 27.28 kcal mol–1, giving the lowest productivity. Controlled-reduction EPR reveals Cu-size-dependent changes in defect-related signals, while transient DRIFTS shows distinct reduction- and treatment-dependent changes in the observable HCOO-related surface pools. Their correspondence with the calculated vacancy energetics and adsorption responses supports a Cu-size-dependent balance among defect formation, reactant activation, and intermediate conversion. Cu clusters couple reactant activation with intermediate conversion to sustain methanol production.

item.title: Selective Formyl Deuteration of Aldehydes by Surface-Enriched Oxygen Vacancy Stabilized Pt on Ceria
item.description:
Abstract
Hydrogen isotope exchange (HIE) is a widely used methodology for deuteration; however, achieving both high isotope abundance and site-selectivity remains challenging for heterogeneous catalysts. Herein, we present a ceria supported platinum catalyst with surface-enriched oxygen vacancy (Ov) that shows impressive formyl deuteration performance with deuterium oxide (D2O) as the deuterium source under hydrogen-free conditions. Using p-methylbenzaldehyde as a model substrate, the typical catalyst achieves >95% deuterium incorporation (D-inc.) at the formyl position while effectively suppressing undesired reductive deuteration pathway. Experimental and theoretical results suggest that the surface-enriched Ov promotes the preferential adsorption of formyl groups on undercoordinated Ce sites, where the local charge redistribution renders the formyl-protons electron-deficient. Simultaneously, the anchored Pt centers effectively catalyze D2O dissociation, generating abundant D* and OD* species. These deuterium species readily interact with the electron-deficient formyl groups, driving hydrogen isotope exchange and forming deuterated aldehydes with high D-formyl selectivity. Substrate scope exploration and gram-scale continuous-flow deuteration experiments demonstrate broad compatibility, revealing its great potential for the selective synthesis of deuterated aldehydes.

item.title: [Graphical abstract added] Mild Heterogeneous Thiophene Hydrogenation Enabled by a Modified Palladium Catalyst
Cation-Regulated Interfacial Proton Transfer for Enhanced C–C Coupling in Electrochemical CO Reduction
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemical CO reduction reaction (CORR) on copper is a prototypical platform for studying C–C coupling toward multicarbon (C2+) products, yet the fundamental factors governing this process remain under debate. Particularly, how electrolyte composition regulates interfacial proton transfer and thereby governs C–C coupling pathways is still unclear. This paper describes the role of alkali metal cations in controlling C–C coupling in CORR by restructuring interfacial water and modulating proton transfer dynamics on Cu electrodes. By varying cation identity (Li+, Na+, K+, Cs+) and concentration, we demonstrate that cations with intrinsic larger ionic radii in the electrolyte shift selectivity toward C2+ products. Combining differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) analysis with in situ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) and attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) investigations, it is revealed that alkali metal cations with large intrinsic radii have weak hydration shells that disrupt the interfacial hydrogen-bond (H-bond) network and increase the population of cation-coordinated water molecules at the interface, which may serve as more effective proton transfer channels toward surface intermediates. This reconstruction of interfacial water can accelerate *CO hydrogenation, thus promoting the C–C coupling for C2+ production. These findings identify interfacial water as an active regulator of interfacial proton transfer, thereby supporting a mechanistic link between electrolyte composition and C–C coupling pathways. This work emphasizes the importance of the interfacial microenvironment and molecular-level understanding of electrochemical reactions.

item.title: Deconstructive Oxygenation of Cyclic Amines by Copper-Catalyzed C(sp 3 )–C(sp 3 ) Bond Cleavage
item.description:
Abstract
Herein, we report a copper-catalyzed deconstructive oxygenation platform for the direct conversion of unstrained N-unsubstituted cyclic amines into versatile β-, γ-, and δ-aminoketones. The product diversity is achieved by adjusting the substituents at the β- or γ-position of cyclic amines that proceed through single or consecutive C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond cleavage, respectively. Following this method, we achieved skeletal modification of unstrained cyclic amines through ring contraction or atom replacement, leading to rapid structural diversification of cyclic amines. The synthetic utility of this method was further demonstrated by the efficient synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant molecules, fluoxetine, atomoxetine, and norfluoxetine. Control experiments indicated that, in the presence of the co-oxidant nitroxyl, the copper-catalyzed sequential dehydrogenative oxidation followed by single-electron transfer-induced aerobic oxygenative C–C bond cleavage was responsible for this effective transformation.

item.title: Cation-Gated Interfacial Electrocatalysis: Mechanisms and Effects of Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metal Cations
item.description:
Abstract
Electrolyte cations, long considered inert charge-balancing species, are now recognized as active regulators of electrocatalytic interfaces. This review systematically examines alkali metal cations (Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+) and alkaline earth metal cations (Mg2+, Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+) in five key reactions: hydrogen evolution/oxidation, oxygen evolution, oxygen reduction, carbon dioxide reduction, and nitrate reduction. We demonstrate that cation effects are reaction-specific, governed by electric double layer structure, interfacial electric fields, local pH, water networks, and intermediate stabilization. Alkali metal cations mainly regulate reactant access, proton transfer, pathway selection, and stability through electric-field modulation, solvation restructuring, intermediate stabilization, and, over longer timescales, catalyst-surface evolution. Hydration characteristics dictate their behavior: weakly hydrated large cations (K+, Rb+, Cs+) enhance local electric fields and stabilize polar intermediates in CO2RR, while strongly hydrated small cations (Li+, Na+) support water dissociation and proton transfer in HER/HOR. Alkaline earth metal cations exhibit chemically coupled interfacial regulation due to higher charge density, stronger hydration, and greater Lewis acidity. These divalent cations facilitate reactions through local pH buffering, water rearrangement, and intermediate stabilization, yet their hydrolysis and precipitation tendencies risk active site blockage and catalyst deactivation, particularly in real electrolytes like seawater and wastewater. By mapping diverse microscopic cation effects onto these five catalytic functions, this review provides a cross-reaction framework for rationalizing apparently contradictory cation trends and identifying the dominant interfacial bottleneck under different conditions. Finally, we highlight future directions in operando characterization, multiscale modeling, multi-ion systems, and electrolyte-catalyst co-design for efficient, selective, and stable electrocatalysis.

item.title: Electrochemical Nitrogen Reduction to Ammonia with Mesoporous Molybdenum-Carbon Electrocatalysts in a Gas Diffusion Flow Cell
item.description:
Abstract
Commercialization of electrochemical nitrogen reduction (eNRR) is hindered by limited catalyst performance, the lack of scalable electrochemical cell architectures, and an incomplete understanding of performance-limiting processes. This work aims to address these challenges through a systematic investigation of catalyst composition and microstructure, device configuration, and reaction mechanisms. Molybdenum (Mo) metal single atoms and clusters supported on mesoporous nitrogen-doped carbon were synthesized with tunable pore sizes via a five-second photothermal pyrolysis of a self-assembled bottlebrush block copolymer (BBCP) template. For eNRR, improved Mo dispersion enhanced electrochemical accessibility, while the coexistence of atomically dispersed Mo species and Mo clusters produced a structurally heterogeneous catalytic environment that benefits eNRR. A gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) flow cell was constructed for continuous operation testing; the catalyst–device system achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 21.6% and an ammonia yield rate of 34.7 μg h–1 mg–1. Intermediate pore sizes and balanced electrode wettability promoted effective triple-phase boundary formation and active-site utilization. Electrochemical characterization combined with machine-learning analysis of flow-cell parameters indicated that activation polarization is the dominant loss mechanism, governed primarily by intrinsic active-site kinetics and electrochemically accessible surface area. In contrast, pore size, metal dispersion, and electrode wettability primarily regulate site accessibility rather than mass-transport limitations. Together, these results provide a framework linking catalyst structure, electrode architecture, and kinetic limitations in eNRR flow-cell systems and offer practical design guidelines for advancing scalable eNRR technology.

item.title: Mild Heterogeneous Thiophene Hydrogenation Enabled by a Modified Palladium Catalyst
item.description:
Abstract
Thiophenes are readily available sulfur heteroarenes and prominent motifs in medicinal and synthetic chemistry, but their direct heterogeneous hydrogenation to thiolanes remains challenging due to sulfur-induced catalyst deactivation and competing hydrodesulfurization. Here, we report a chloroform-induced surface modification strategy that enables the heterogeneous Pd(OH)2/C-catalyzed hydrogenation of thiophenes to saturated sulfur heterocycles. The method proceeds under mild hydrogenation conditions and provides access to a range of alkyl-, silyl-, aryl-, and benzofused thiolane derivatives. A hydrogenation-focused robustness assessment revealed compatibility with several functional groups that are commonly sensitive under Pd/H2 conditions, while preparative scope studies showed that functional-group-containing thiophenes can be converted when potentially interfering motifs are separated from the thiophene core by suitable alkyl or aryl spacers. Mechanistic experiments indicate that CHCl3 is not merely a beneficial solvent: CHCl3/H2 pretreatment of Pd(OH)2/C generates a catalytically competent material whose activity is retained after replacing CHCl3 with 2-MeTHF. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) analyses support the formation of persistent chloroform-derived organochlorine/C–Cl-type surface environments and chlorocarbon fragments. These findings establish solvent-induced catalyst modification as a useful design principle for challenging heterogeneous hydrogenations of sulfur-containing heteroarenes.

item.title: Diffusion-Selective Modulation Strategy for Enhanced Propane Dehydrogenation via Mixing Inert CHA Zeolite
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving a high propane conversion in propane dehydrogenation to propylene (PDH) carries tremendous scientific and economic value, particularly if achievable with established industrial units. Here we propose a diffusion-selective modulation strategy driven by large-scale machine-learning computation, where the key to success lies in finding auxiliary materials to drive the PDH reaction forward by enlarging the diffusion-rate difference between H2 and C3 species. This strategy is demonstrated theoretically via high-throughput computation and then validated experimentally through the introduction of inert siliceous CHA zeolites as a diffusion-selective modulator within the catalyst bed. By simply physically mixing CHA with various PDH catalysts, we show that the single-pass propane conversion can increase by 1–5% from industrial space velocities (10 h–1) to significantly higher throughputs (256 h–1), consistently improving performance across multiple reported catalysts without compromising stability. This “plug-and-play” methodology can be directly implemented in existing industrial PDH units without altering either the catalyst formulation or the reactor configuration, providing a readily implementable and scalable route for upgrading current PDH infrastructure.

item.title: Curvature-Induced Electric-Field Effects Govern Controllable N 2 Electrocatalysis on Single-Atom Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Electric field-enhanced electrocatalysis represents an innovative strategy for improving the efficiency of electrochemical transformations. However, quantitative evaluation of microscopic electric-field effects under operando conditions remains challenging, limiting a rigorous, predictive understanding of field-mediated reaction regulation. Here, by integrating rigorous numerical methods, constant-potential microkinetic simulations, and machine learning models, we establish electric-field intensity as a quantitative descriptor that directly correlates local fields with catalytic performance. Using curvature-engineered M–N–C single-atom catalysts as a model platform, we demonstrate that curvature-induced electric fields modulate electron occupation at active sites and shift the potential of zero charge in a controllable manner. This field-driven electronic perturbation selectively tunes adsorbate binding energetics, thereby dictating limiting potentials, steering reaction pathways, and governing the thermodynamics and kinetics of interfacial proton-coupled electron transfer in nitrogen electroreduction. Notably, we uncover an inverted volcano–type dependence of catalytic activity on curvature, wherein optimal activity is achieved within a moderate field-strength window. This nonmonotonic trend underscores the necessity of balanced curvature regulation, rather than simply maximizing field intensity, in optimizing electrocatalytic performance. These findings provide a quantitative framework for monitoring and regulating catalytic trends under realistic operating conditions via curvature-induced electric fields, offering generalizable design principles for diverse SAC systems and electrochemical reactions.

item.title: CNT-Mediated Integration of Pd and In 2 O 3 Circumvents Activity–Stability Trade-Off in CO 2 Hydrogenation to Methanol
item.description:
Abstract
Metal promotion is a widely adopted strategy to enhance the activity of indium oxide (In2O3) catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation to methanol. However, intimately contacted metal promoters on In2O3 often result in rapid catalyst deactivation, as excessive local H2 supply induces undesirable structural degradation of the In2O3 domain. Here, we address this limitation by implementing a carbon nanotube (CNT)-mediated hydrogen transport pathway, which spatially separates the H2 activation sites (Pd) from the CO2 hydrogenation sites (In2O3) at the catalyst preparation stage. Intriguingly, upon reductive activation, the initially separated components spontaneously evolve into a distinctive interfacial configuration. In this configuration, InOx migrates onto and partially covers the Pd nanoparticles, forming an InOx@Pd inverse interface. Unlike the directly constructed Pd–In2O3 interface, which suffers from over-reduction to metallic In0 accompanied by sintering and alloying with Pd, this CNT-derived interface preserves the In3+ oxidation state and serves as a non-destructive junction for hydrogen delivery. Combined with long-range hydrogen spillover across the CNT network, this architecture transforms a concentrated and destructive hydrogen flux into a regulated supply that reaches distal In2O3 domains without driving over-reduction. Consequently, the Pd/CNT + In2O3 system exhibits both improved catalytic activity and enhanced long-term stability (>230 h), whereas the conventional Pd/In2O3 catalyst deactivates continuously. These findings demonstrate that a controlled hydrogen delivery system between H2 activation sites and active sites on the oxide domain offers an effective way for developing active and durable catalysts involving reduction-sensitive oxide phases.

item.title: Hydration Changes are Essential for Efficient Breakdown of Faropenem by the L1 Metallo-β-lactamase
item.description:
Abstract
Metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) are key contributors to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The L1 MBL, originally from Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, is a tetrameric, dizinc, subclass B3 MBL that efficiently hydrolyzes most β-lactam antibiotics and evades inhibitors that act on other MBLs. Using quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (DFTB3/MM) simulations with enhanced sampling, we mapped the full reaction pathway and minimum free energy profile for L1-catalyzed hydrolysis of faropenem, a penem antibiotic whose reaction can yield alternative enamine and imine products. Benchmarking against B3LYP-D3/6-31G(d) shows that DFTB3 provides the best correlation between energy and structure for this system. We test different possible mechanisms and find that changes in hydration at the metal site during the catalytic cycle are critical for efficient hydrolysis. Our results show that a zinc-bridging hydroxide acts as the nucleophile, with the conserved active site residue D120 participating in back-and-forth proton-transfer events and stabilizing the enzyme-intermediate (EI) complex. The direct reaction of EI, however, involves a large energy barrier; the second stage is facilitated by diffusion of a water molecule into the active site. This water molecule was observed during long-timescale MM MD simulations using the Extended Zinc Amber Force Field (EZAFF). Direct proton transfer from this water to the substrate amide nitrogen forms an enamine product, while imine formation requires rotation of the faropenem 6α-hydroxyethyl substituent to enable proton transfer from water to the substrate C2. The calculated free energy barriers for the formation of both products are consistent with the experimentally determined catalytic constant, and the calculated greater stability of the imine with its crystallographic observation. These simulations provide dynamic insight into L1 catalysis, highlighting features that can be exploited for inhibitor design.

item.title: Crystal Phase-Dependent Electronic Metal-Support Interactions Enable Chemoselective Hydrogenation of α, β-Unsaturated Aldehydes
item.description:
Abstract
Electronic metal-support interactions (EMSI) provide an effective means of tuning the electronic structure of supported metal catalysts and thereby modulating their catalytic properties. However, how the crystal phase of supports governs EMSI and in turn influences the selective hydrogenation remains largely unexplored. Here, we report a crystal-phase engineering strategy to precisely regulate EMSI in ultrafine Ir nanoclusters (NCs) supported on polymorphic Nb2O5. Comprehensive spectroscopic characterization reveals that the orthorhombic Nb2O5-T phase forms a distinctive socketed metal-support interface that strongly anchors Ir NCs and induces substantial electron transfer from the support to the metal. Distinct from classical strong metal-support interactions that often compromise active-site accessibility, this socketed interfacial configuration simultaneously enhances EMSI, stabilizes the Ir NCs, and preserves abundant exposed active sites. The resulting electron-rich Ir species facilitates H2 activation and interfacial hydrogen spillover while favoring preferential adsorption of the carbonyl group over the C=C bond in α, β-unsaturated aldehydes. Consequently, Ir@Nb2O5-T exhibits high activity, selectivity, and durability for the selective hydrogenation to unsaturated alcohols under mild conditions, overcoming the typical activity–selectivity trade-off. This work establishes a direct crystal phase–EMSI–reactivity relationship and highlights crystal-phase engineering as a powerful strategy for manipulating metal–support interfaces toward highly selective heterogeneous catalysis.

item.title: Enhanced Aqueous-Phase Hydrodeoxygenation of Fatty Acids over CoP Anchored on P–N Co-Doped Carbon
item.description:
Abstract
The aqueous-phase hydrodeoxygenation of biomass-derived fatty acids offers an alternative route for the production of diesel-range hydrocarbons, but remains a major challenge. Herein, we report a hydrophobic CoP catalyst anchored on P–N co-doped carbon spheres (CoP@PNC-900), which exhibits high performance for the aqueous-phase hydrodeoxygenation of palmitic acid at 270 °C and 2 MPa H2, delivering nearly complete conversion together with over 99% yield of C15+C16 alkanes. The enhanced performance arises from the synergy between CoP active sites and the hydrophobic interface, which promotes C–O bond cleavage while enhancing the contact between hydrophobic substrates and catalytic sites. Isotopic-labeling experiments demonstrate that water acts exclusively as the reaction medium rather than a hydrogen source. In situ FT-IR–MS analysis combined with DFT calculations confirms the hydrodeoxygenation- and decarbonylation-related pathways, with C–O bond cleavage of the alcohol intermediate identified as the rate-determining step in the hydrodeoxygenation pathway. Moreover, the catalyst exhibits a broad substrate scope for various fatty acids and esters as well as stable recyclability under hydrothermal conditions. Finally, a preliminary life cycle assessment (LCA) highlights the potential environmental benefits of the aqueous-phase catalytic process. This work establishes an effective strategy that integrates active-site engineering with interfacial hydrophobic microenvironment regulation for the aqueous-phase valorization of biomass-derived fatty acids.

item.title: Proton-Donor Identity Shapes Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction on Silver
item.description:
Abstract
Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction is a key reaction in nitrogen cycling and water remediation, yet the mechanistic interpretation of its voltammetric response remains poorly understood. On silver electrodes, cyclic voltammograms often display multiple cathodic features assigned to different reaction steps, although a consistent mechanistic interpretation remains elusive. Here, we combine cyclic voltammetry analysis with in situ product detection using scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM), and hydrodynamic analysis using rotating disk electrode (RDE), to investigate nitrate-to-nitrite electroreduction on silver. We show that the cathodic response changes from a single peak to two distinct features with increasing nitrate concentration when using phosphate buffer as a supporting electrolyte. Analysis of concentration, scan rate, and pH dependencies, together with systematic variation of phosphate electrolyte composition, indicates that these features arise from distinct interfacial proton-transfer regimes associated with the availability of H2PO4– as a proton donor. In addition, SECM enables the assignment of each feature to local nitrite formation, ruling out changes in product identity as the origin of each feature. These findings show that phosphate electrolyte modulates proton-donor availability, and, consequently, the voltammetric response of nitrate reduction on silver, providing a framework for interpreting the complex electrocatalytic behavior observed in this system.

item.title: Synthesis of Chiral α-Aminophosphonate Derivatives through Copper(I)-Catalyzed Enantioselective Alkylation
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient methodologies for the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of α-aminophosphonic acid derivatives remain limited, particularly those involving carbon-carbon (C-C) bond formation. Herein, we report a copper(I)-catalyzed enantioselective alkylation of N-protected aminomethylthiophosphonates with alkyl halides, which provides a versatile strategy for accessing diverse chiral α-aminophosphonate derivatives. A wide range of alkyl halides, including allyl bromides, propargyl bromide, benzyl bromides, and alkyl iodides, act as efficient alkylating agents. Control experiments demonstrate that the employment of the 9H-fluoren-9-ylidene group and the incorporation of a sulfur atom into the phosphonate moiety are crucial for facilitating efficient deprotonation. NMR studies indicate that N-protected aminomethylthiophosphonate undergoes effective chelation with the copper(I) catalyst, a process that plays a pivotal role in promoting the reaction. Finally, both cleavage of the imine moiety and oxidation of the thiophosphonate group can be readily achieved under mild reaction conditions.

item.title: LiH/FePcG-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis via Interfacial Hydride-Mediated Dinitrogen Activation
item.description:
Abstract
Ammonia synthesis under mild conditions remains challenging because of the inertness of the N≡N bond and the limited ability of conventional catalysts to couple efficient dinitrogen activation with rapid hydrogenation. Here, we report a LiH/FePcG catalyst in which strong interfacial coupling between LiH and Fe–N–C sites enable efficient ammonia synthesis. Comprehensive characterization, including structural analysis, kinetic study, isotopic-labelling, gas-phase mass spectrometry, and in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) reveal that the catalytic activity originates from interfacial active sites. Under reaction conditions, structural nitrogen atoms within the Fe–Nx moieties undergo reversible consumption and reconstruction, demonstrating the dynamic participation of the Fe–N–C framework in ammonia synthesis. Concurrently, hydridic hydrogen supplied by LiH directly participates in the initial hydrogenation steps, while the LiH/Fe–N–C interface generates Fe-centered multicomponent hydride species essential for N2 binding and activation. An inverse H/D kinetic isotope effect, an H2-promoted 28N2/30N2 exchange rate, in situ spectroscopic evidence, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations collectively support a non-classical, hydrogen-assisted pathway for dinitrogen activation rather than the conventional direct N≡ bond cleavage. These findings establish interfacial hydride chemistry as a cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis and provide a strategy for designing advanced catalysts under mild conditions.

item.title: Engineering the Interfacial Microenvironment to Boost Ethane Dehydrogenation on Ga 2 O 3 -Pt Catalysts via Metal Doping Modulation
item.description:
Abstract
Inverse Ga2O3-Pt catalysts have exhibited better catalytic performance in propane dehydrogenation due to their tunable interfacial electronic properties. This study explores the potential of inverse Ga2O3-Pt catalysts and their single-atom-doped variant (Ga2O3-M/Pt) systems for ethane dehydrogenation using DFT calculations and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. The results show that Ga2O3-Pt exhibits low ethylene formation activity (0.83 × 102 s–1) and selectivity (84.28%) due to its interfacial sites that weakly and uniformly adsorb hydrogen, impeding the differential regulation of key CH2CH3* intermediate adsorption behavior. Single-atom doping (M = Ti, Co, etc.) creates a Pt–M–O interfacial microenvironment, modulating the electronic structure of interfacial oxygen sites, which enables the effective differential regulation of CH2CH3* intermediate adsorption, thereby enhancing catalytic performance. Among the 14 screened dopants, the Ga2O3-Ti/Pt catalyst emerged as optimal, showing high activity (2.86 × 103 s–1) and selectivity (97.13%) for ethylene formation at the optimal 873.15 K and CH3CH3(g) partial pressure of 0.20 bar. This advantage stems from its moderate p-band center and Ti–O charge transfer, which yield an ideal hydrogen adsorption energy for CH2CH3* regulation. The H* adsorption energy can serve as a descriptor for qualitatively evaluating the activity of CH2CH2(g) formation for a series of Ga2O3-M/Pt catalysts. This work proposes the strategy of “interfacial microenvironment reconstruction to regulate the electronic structure” as a design method for developing high-efficiency alkane dehydrogenation catalysts.

item.title: Mechanistic Investigation and Optimization of a Mixed-Oxide@Alkali Carbonate Redox Catalyst Platform for Enhanced Ethane Oxidative Dehydrogenation
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical looping oxidative dehydrogenation (CL-ODH) of ethane has emerged as a promising alternative for ethylene production, with the potential to mitigate the environmental and sustainability concerns associated with conventional steam cracking. The main challenge of CL-ODH is the design of active and selective redox catalysts to enhance ethane activation while minimizing the generation of by-products such as COx (CO and CO2). This study employs ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations to investigate the formation and reactivity of oxygen species in mixed metal-oxides@Li2CO3 and Na2CO3 redox catalysts. Estimated reaction free energies are used as thermodynamic descriptors, while the computational insights are supplemented with experimental validations. Our analysis indicates that peroxide (O22–) and •OH radicals provide more favorable thermodynamic driving forces for ethane C–H activation at the outer carbonate surface than monatomic oxygen radical anion (O–) and superoxide (O2–). In addition, mechanistic investigations into COx formation reveal that the product water can interact with peroxide-derived species at the gas–carbonate interface to generate •OH radicals, consistent with prior experimental observations. In Li2CO3, •OH-mediated pathways retain favorable ethane C─H activation thermodynamics while reducing the driving force for selected COx-forming transformations relative to peroxide. These findings provide important mechanistic insights into the design and optimization of mixed-oxide@alkali carbonate core-shell redox catalysts for CL-ODH.

item.title: Spin Polarization Enables Spin-Conserved Intermediate Migration for Selective C–N Coupling toward Urea Electrosynthesis
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemical coreduction of CO2 and nitrate to urea offers a promising approach to carbon–nitrogen fixation but still suffers from sluggish C–N coupling and severe competition from ammonia formation. Existing studies primarily focus on intermediate adsorption and largely overlook the spin-state changes that occur during intermediate transformation and C–N coupling. Herein, we introduce a Cu-modulated spin-regulation strategy where Cu substitution subtly modulates the Fe electronic configuration of FeSe2 to generate spin-polarized Fe centers. We reveal that mixed-valence Fe species in Cu-FeSe2 induce a double-exchange-like spin polarization, which facilitated the migration of N-containing intermediates between neighboring Fe sites, thereby promoting C–N coupling. As a result, the Cu-FeSe2 catalyst achieves a urea Faradaic efficiency of 54.1%, a yield rate of 78.5 mmol h–1 g–1, and an electrochemical stability over 75 h. Supported by operando spectroscopic analyses and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the spin-polarized Fe centers stabilize *COOH and *NH2 intermediates while suppressing over-hydrogenation to ammonia. This work highlights spin polarization as a promising strategy for constructing efficient electrocatalytic sites and enabling multi-intermediate electrocatalysis toward urea synthesis.

item.title: Directed Electrocatalytic Nitrate Conversion via H-Bond Network Fortification
item.description:
Abstract
Electrocatalytic reduction of nitrate (NO3–) is highly desired for the synthesis of value-added nitrogenous compounds, where precise selectivity control remains as a key challenge to be tackled. In addition to catalyst composition, electrolyte microenvironment offers another feasible handle for selectivity regulation, where the interfacial H-bond network could be effectively tuned for directed H-atom transfer for selectivity manipulation. Herein, two molecules with distinct molecular configurations, oxalic acid (OA) and acetic acid (HOAc), were introduced into the electrolyte microenvironment to investigate the in-depth structure-functional relationship between electrolyte structure and electrocatalytic NO3– selectivity, where vicinal H-bond acceptors (carboxylic groups) makes OA an ideal “molecular glue” to fortify the H-bond network for H atom transfer. As a result, OA significantly facilitates electrocatalytic NO3– hydrogenation, leading to efficient production of NH2OH (219 μmol·cm–2·h–1, 78.2%). Contrastingly, partially hydrogenated NO2– is characterized as the major product upon HOAc introduction (284.4 μmol·cm–2·h–1, 82.4%), which lacks vicinal carboxylic groups for H-bond network fortification. The NH2OH and NO2– products were effectively converted to formaldoxime and nitrophenol, which extended the directed electrocatalytic NO3– conversion toward synthetic applications.

item.title: Efficient Photocatalytic H 2 O 2 Formation by a Porphyrin-TiO 2 Hybrid Catalyst in Pure Water
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient production of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) has attracted much interest because of the growing importance of H2O2 as an energy source. In this study, we have developed photocatalytic H2O2 production in ultrapure water catalyzed by an organic–inorganic hybrid photocatalyst. The hybrid photocatalyst was prepared by immobilizing a diprotonated dodecaphenylporphyrin derivative (H4DPP2+-C) having carboxyl groups at the periphery to be anchored on a TiO2 surface. Photoirradiation to the hybrid photocatalyst (H4DPP2+-C/TiO2) dispersed in ultrapure water resulted in efficient H2O2 production by O2 reduction, as confirmed by iodometry for the supernatant. The concentration of aqueous H2O2 was determined to be 0.30 mM after 1 min of photoirradiation and the initial rate of H2O2 formation by H4DPP2+-C/TiO2 was determined to be 29 mmol g–1 h–1, which was higher than previously reported values in ultrapure water without any sacrificial reagents. In addition, the external quantum yield at 365 nm reached 27%, which is the highest value among semiconductor photocatalysts for H2O2 production. Based on the results from femtosecond transient reflectance spectroscopy, photoinduced electron transfer from the conduction band of photoexcited TiO2 to H4DPP2+-C on TiO2 was confirmed to afford the one-electron reduced species of H4DPP2+-C, which is further reduced to form a putative isophlorin intermediate as a two-electron reduced species to reduce O2 for H2O2 formation. Thus, H4DPP2+-C/TiO2 performs water oxidation at the TiO2 surface to gain electrons and two-electron reduction of O2 at the H4DPP2+-C moiety, respectively.

item.title: Varying Mechanisms Dominate Formate Formation in Electrochemical CO 2 Reduction on Cu, Au, and Pb: A Constant Potential DFT-Based Microkinetic Analysis
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemical CO2 reduction offers a route to convert renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals while closing the anthropogenic carbon cycle. However, the technology struggles to surpass the lab scale as it is limited by low selectivity and energy efficiency. These challenges are less severe for the two-electron products, carbon monoxide and formate, making them attractive targets. Formate is of particular interest due to its potential as an energy carrier and its relatively high market value. Yet its formation mechanism remains debated, hindering rational catalyst design. Here, we combine grand canonical DFT, a hybrid explicit-implicit solvent model, and microkinetic simulations to elucidate the formate formation mechanism on Cu, Au, and Pb, and show that distinct pathways dominate on each metal. On Cu, formate formation proceeds via O-bound chemisorption of CO2 followed by protonation. Au exhibits negligible formate activity despite supporting different formate pathways depending on facet termination and applied potential, as these pathways remain kinetically unfavorable. Finally, Pb facilitates a direct outer-sphere-like process from physisorbed CO2 to formate, with high activity. The enhanced activity may originate from the distinct electronic structure of Pb, characterized by diffuse p-like states near the Fermi level, a feature shared by other formate-selective post-transition-metal catalysts. The variation in mechanisms for formate production likely underlies the difficulty of identifying universal activity descriptors for electrochemical CO2 and suggests that catalyst design might necessitate mechanism-specific descriptors.

item.title: Early Transition Metal Carbene Complexes as Photocatalysts: Unveiling Dual-Emission and Photo-reactivity
item.description:
Abstract
Photoactive transition metal complexes are playing a pivotal role in synthetic chemistry and application technologies, such as photocatalysis and light-emitting diodes, yet they often depend on precious metals. Early-transition-metal photosensitizers offer a promising, yet still highly challenging, alternative, and understanding of their excited-state behavior is crucial for the design of more efficient compounds. Here, we present a detailed photophysical and computational study of homoleptic N-heterocyclic carbene [OCO]-type zirconium and hafnium d0 complexes, revealing their potential as efficient Earth-abundant photocatalysts. Steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopy, combined with (TD-)DFT calculations, uncover dual emission pathways involving both singlet and triplet states. Variable-temperature photoluminescence studies demonstrate that these emissions arise from distinct excited states rather than thermally activated delayed fluorescence. Under UV irradiation, both complexes catalyze bromo-alkylation of alkenes with various bromoalkyls, including fluorinated reagents, to access diverse molecular scaffolds. Mechanistic investigations incorporating Stern–Volmer quenching analysis, quantum yield measurements, and variable time normalization analyses (VTNA) support a photoinduced electron transfer process within the proposed catalytic cycle.

item.title: Blocking, Widening, Regulating, and Tailoring-Based Engineering of an Imine Reductase for Asymmetric Reductive Amination of Sterically Demanding Ketones with Ammonia
item.description:
Abstract
Chiral amines are essential building blocks for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals. Although imine reductases (IREDs) have emerged as powerful biocatalysts for chiral amine synthesis, their application in reductive amination using ammonia as an amino donor remains limited, especially for sterically demanding ketone substrates. Herein, we developed a BWRT (Blocking, Widening, Regulating, and Tailoring) strategy for engineering the active-site pocket of an IRED from Saccharopolyspora erythraea (SeIRED). The engineered variant, SeIRED-M4, containing 17 amino acid mutations, exhibited a 23,300-fold increase in specific activity along with a 19 °C increase in melting temperature (Tm) relative to the wild-type enzyme. SeIRED-M4 efficiently catalyzed the asymmetric reductive amination of a broad range of ketones with ammonia, affording the corresponding chiral amines with up to 98% conversion and >99% ee. The synthetic applicability of SeIRED-M4 was further demonstrated through the gram-scale synthesis of sitagliptin ((R)-1b), achieving 93% conversion and >99% ee at a substrate loading of up to 40 g/L. Collectively, this study demonstrates an active-site engineering strategy that improves catalytic performance by regulating substrate accessibility and productive binding orientation, highlighting the importance of controlling substrate-binding conformations in biocatalyst development for pharmaceutical applications.

item.title: Enantiocomplementary Total Biosynthesis of Cyclic Imino Acids Enabled by an S N 2 Reaction Catalyzed by a Class I Aldolase and a Transaminase
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclic noncanonical imino acids are highly valuable in drug design due to their rigid conformational constraints. However, their structural complexity has limited the development of robust synthetic methods. Herein, we report a concise strategy for the enantiocomplementary total synthesis of these compounds. This route is driven by two key biocatalytic steps: a non-natural SN2 reaction catalyzed by a class I pyruvate aldolase, followed by an enantiocomplementary reductive amination catalyzed by amino acid transaminases. We successfully implement this synthesis in E. coli whole-cell catalysts for streamlined production. From simple precursors, we synthesize 42 cyclic imino acids, including the natural product proferrorosamine A, in yields of up to 98% and with enantioselectivity up to >99% ee. This work underscores the potential of leveraging non-natural activities of class I aldolases to create concise enzymatic routes for synthesizing complex chiral heterocycles beyond imino acids.

item.title: Regiodivergent Oxyfuctionalization of Non-natural Tricyclic Terpenoids Using Sequence Divergent Unspecific Peroxygenases (UPOs)
item.description:
Abstract
Unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) catalyze the H2O2-dependent monooxygenation of organic substrates with regioselectivity and chemoselectivity; however, their application to sterically demanding, non-natural terpene skeletons has remained largely unexplored to date. Here, we present a computationally-guided, multiparametric screening pipeline that was used to prioritize 17 structurally distinct UPOs and UPO-like enzymes for the late-stage oxyfunctionalization of chemoenzymatically synthesized tricyclic terpenoids not reported from natural sources. These are accessible via BcBOT2-catalyzed cyclization of non-natural farnesyl diphosphate analogs. The computer-aided pre-screening included an evaluation of expression levels, an analysis of the tunnel architecture for substrate access, and hierarchical docking using geometric criteria close to the attack conformation to rank candidate enzymes. Experimental screening of the prioritized enzymes identified productive UPO-substrate combinations showed correspondence between the docking-based regioselectivity predictions and the product profiles confirmed by GC–MS. MthUPO FuncLib_18 catalyzed an “orchestrated” linear cascade of three consecutive oxidations of a furan sesquiterpenoid, converting it into an α-hydroxylactone—a transformation that mimics the natural oxidative diversification that biosynthetically follows terpene cyclization. In addition, a single inversion of the stereocenter in the furano sesquiterpenoids diastereomer pair redirected the regioselectivity of MspUPO-mg133 and ChiUPO-II to opposite sides of the furan ring. This finding thus represents a proof-of-concept for regioselectivity reversal through stereochemical changes in the substrate during UPO-catalyzed terpenoid oxidation. Additionally, we were able to access two structures with tertiary alcohols, difficult to achieve by chemical means. In silico comparison of AlphaFold 3 models, supported by multiple-sequence alignment, suggested that the Monosporascus UPOs characterized here form a distinct UPO/UPO-like subgroup characterized by an EHR catalytic motif, a shortened α-helix, an elongated loop, and an active-site lacking aromatic residues and exhibit comparatively the lowest predicted active-site hydrophobicity among all characterized UPOs. Molecular dynamics simulations, combined with an analysis of the near-attack-conformations of selected enzyme-substrate complexes, confirmed that only the experimentally observed oxidation positions achieve sustained proximity to the ferryl oxygen of compound I with catalytically suitable approach angles over timescales in the microsecond timescale. This work thus expands both the known sequence-structure space of catalytically competent UPOs and the accessible chemical space of terpenoids as substrates.

item.title: Mechanistic Characterization of Mollisia scopiformis Mycolaurene Synthase, an Enzyme Showing Little but Decisive Intermediate Stabilization
item.description:
Abstract
A fungal multiproduct sesquiterpene synthase from Mollisia scopiformis (MsMS), a laurane-type sesquiterpene synthase that generates a 6/5 bicyclic skeleton, is reported. Using a combination of experimental and theoretical techniques, including isotopic labelings, DFT calculations, molecular docking, site-directed mutagenesis, and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we elucidated the detailed enzyme mechanisms diverging from the (S)-bisabolyl cation as a central intermediate toward all the observed products.
